title: South Carolina Security Deposit Rules
bodyText:
South Carolina sets no limit on the size of a security deposit and does not require interest, a separate or escrow account, or a notice of where the deposit is held. A security deposit is money the landlord holds in trust to secure the tenant's performance.

When the tenancy ends, the landlord may keep only accrued rent and damages caused by the tenant's failure to meet the tenant's statutory and lease duties, and must send an itemized written notice of deductions with any refund within 30 days after the tenancy ends and the tenant delivers possession, or after the tenant demands the deposit, whichever is later. The tenant must give a forwarding address in writing; a landlord with no notice of the tenant's whereabouts may mail to the last known address.

A landlord who fails to return prepaid rent or the deposit with the required notice can owe three times the amount wrongfully withheld plus attorney's fees.

A landlord renting more than four adjoining units who uses different deposit standards must post or hand out those standards before the lease is signed. On a sale, the seller stays liable for the deposit unless it is transferred to the buyer and the tenant is told in writing.

Real estate brokers and property managers must keep tenant deposits in a trust or escrow account. A landlord renting more than four adjoining units who uses different standards to set deposits must give each tenant a written statement of those standards before the lease is signed (S.C. Code Ann. 27-40-410(c)); the lease's optional clause records it.

title: Repair Duties and Tenant Remedies
bodyText:
A South Carolina landlord must comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, make all repairs needed to keep the property fit and habitable, keep common areas reasonably safe (and reasonably clean in buildings of more than four units), supply running water, reasonable hot water and heat, and maintain supplied electrical, gas, plumbing, heating, air-conditioning and other facilities and appliances, including elevators.

A tenant may not waive these duties, except that a single-family tenant may agree in writing to take on appliance and facility maintenance and specified tasks.

If the landlord materially fails, the tenant may give written notice that the lease will end in at least 14 days unless the breach is fixed. If the landlord negligently or wilfully fails to supply essential services, the tenant may, after written notice, buy reasonable amounts of the service and deduct the cost from rent, or recover the drop in rental value.

South Carolina does not allow a tenant to repair and deduct, and a mechanic's lien from repairs the tenant orders without consent is unenforceable. A tenant who wants to raise a repair problem as a defense to nonpayment generally must have given notice at least 14 days before rent was due (or, for essential services, in time for emergency repairs).

If a fire or casualty substantially impairs the unit, the tenant may leave and end the lease on 7 days' written notice, or stay in the usable part at reduced rent. Landlord interruption of essential services or ouster costs three months' rent or twice actual damages, whichever is greater, plus fees.

title: Eviction (Ejectment) Process
bodyText: South Carolina evictions are 'ejectment' cases in magistrate court. For nonpayment, the landlord may end the lease if rent is not paid within five days of the due date after a written notice of nonpayment and intent to terminate; a notice in bold, conspicuous type in the written lease satisfies this for the whole tenancy, including any month-to-month continuation. For other breaches that can be fixed, the landlord gives written notice allowing 14 days to cure. The magistrate issues a rule requiring the tenant to vacate or show cause within 10 days after service; service may be made by posting and mailing after two failed attempts. If the tenant does not appear, or loses, the magistrate issues a writ, and the officer gives the occupants 24 hours to leave before removing them. A tenant who raises defenses must pay rent into court as it comes due. Accepting rent after the rule is issued does not waive the eviction. From 2026-06-30, an appeal stays the eviction only if the tenant files an affidavit promising to pay rent as it comes due. The landlord recovers attorney's fees only if represented by an attorney and the tenant's nonpayment was not in good faith or other breach was wilful. The eviction notice must tell the tenant that belongings put on the street will be removed after 48 hours. Eviction and default notices under a lease for a primary residence are outside South Carolina's electronic-transactions law, so they should be delivered on paper. From 2027, eviction records are removed from public indexes after seven years. Where the lease's bold notice satisfies the nonpayment notice for the whole tenancy, the lease doesn't promise a fresh written notice for each late payment; you may still give one before ending the lease. If the property has a federally backed mortgage or is in a covered federal housing program, give the 30-day notice to vacate described in `edu-cares-act-notice` before filing, even though the lease's statutory nonpayment paragraph says no other notice will be given.

title: No Self-Help Eviction
bodyText: A South Carolina landlord may not recover possession by changing the locks, removing the tenant or the tenant's belongings, or wilfully interrupting essential services such as water, heat, electricity or gas, except after abandonment, surrender or a court eviction. A tenant who is unlawfully removed or excluded, or whose essential services are wilfully interrupted, may recover possession or end the lease and recover three months' rent or twice actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees, and the deposit must be returned. A lease clause giving the landlord a lien on the tenant's household goods is unenforceable; rent can be collected by distress only through the magistrate's statutory procedure.

title: Retaliation
bodyText: A South Carolina landlord may not retaliate against a tenant who complained to a code-enforcement agency about a health-and-safety violation, or to the landlord about a violation of the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, by raising rent above fair-market value, cutting essential services, or suing for possession. Exceptions include a violation the tenant caused, the tenant's own material noncompliance, and code work that would require vacating the unit. A landlord renting more than four adjoining units may raise rent uniformly for all tenants without a presumption of retaliation. A retaliatory non-renewal of a tenant who is current on rent can delay recovery of possession for 75 days; the statute is written for refusing to renew a lease that expires and does not say how it applies when a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy is ended by notice. Retaliation exposes the landlord to up to three months' rent or treble damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees; a tenant who raises the defense in bad faith can owe the landlord the same. A tenant must notify the landlord in writing within 10 days after service of the rule to vacate if the tenant will raise retaliation as a defense. A protected domestic-violence tenant who ends the lease under South Carolina law is also protected from retaliation.

title: Ending a Periodic Tenancy
bodyText: Unless the lease sets a definite term, a South Carolina tenancy is month-to-month (week-to-week for a roomer paying weekly). Either party may end a month-to-month tenancy by written notice given at least 30 days before the termination date in the notice, and a week-to-week tenancy by written notice at least 7 days before. A tenancy for a fixed term ends at the end of the term without notice. A month-to-month tenancy does not become year-to-year. A lease cannot shorten the tenant's statutory notice.

title: Holdover Remedies
bodyText:
If a South Carolina tenant stays after the lease ends without the landlord's consent, the landlord may bring an action for possession. If the holdover is not in good faith, the landlord may also recover attorney's fees, and if it is a wilful violation of the Act or the lease, up to three months' periodic rent or twice actual damages, whichever is greater, plus fees.

If the landlord consents to the tenant staying, the tenancy becomes month-to-month (week-to-week for a roomer who pays weekly rent) unless the lease fixes a definite term.

Older general statutes also provide double the value of the premises for a tenant who holds over three months after a written demand for possession, and double rent for a tenant who gives written notice to quit and then does not leave; they apply to residential leases only where consistent with the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act.

title: Servicemember Rights
bodyText: Servicemembers renting in South Carolina have the lease-termination and eviction protections of the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act. South Carolina's own Servicemembers Civil Relief Act makes any violation of the federal Act a violation of state law, extends coverage to South Carolina National Guard members called to state active duty for more than 30 consecutive days and to other states' Guard members on similar duty, gives dependents the same rights, and lets a servicemember, a dependent or the Attorney General sue for an injunction, restitution and a civil penalty of up to $5,000 per intentional violation. South Carolina's separate military contract-termination right covers telecommunications, internet, television, gym and satellite radio contracts, not leases.

title: South Carolina Fair Housing Law
bodyText: The South Carolina Fair Housing Law bars housing discrimination because of race, color, religion, sex, familial status, national origin or handicap, including discriminatory advertising, and requires reasonable accommodations and, at the tenant's expense, reasonable modifications for a disability. It exempts an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units and, in limited cases, an individual owner renting a single-family house without a broker or discriminatory advertising, though the advertising ban still applies. A landlord may refuse someone who poses a real and present threat of substantial harm, may act on a conviction for illegal manufacture or distribution of a controlled substance, and may ask on the application about the number, ages, sex and relationships of intended occupants and about such convictions. A separate statute bars discrimination against a handicapped person in housing without reasonable justification. South Carolina law adds no protected class beyond the federal ones, does not protect source of income, and has no statute limiting a landlord's inquiry into immigration status or restricting firearms in private rentals.

title: Service Animal and Assistance Dog Law
bodyText:
In South Carolina a person with a disability who has an assistance dog is entitled to full and equal access to rental housing with the dog, and may not be charged extra for it, though the person is liable for any damage the dog causes.

For other assistance animals, including emotional support animals, a landlord may ask two questions (whether the person has a disability that substantially limits a major life activity, and whether the person has a disability-related need for the animal) and may request documentation, which is sufficient if it shows a disability and that the animal provides disability-related assistance or emotional support.

State law defines a service animal as a dog or miniature horse trained to do disability-related work, and says emotional support is not such work. Knowingly misrepresenting an animal as a service animal to obtain a disabled person's rights is punishable by a civil fine of up to $250 for a first offense, $500 for a second and $1,000 after that; it is not a crime.

title: Local Rent Control Preemption
bodyText: South Carolina counties and cities may not regulate in any way the amount of rent charged for privately owned single-family, multi-unit residential or commercial rental property. They may regulate rent on their own property and by agreement with private owners. State law does not otherwise preempt local housing, registration, inspection or source-of-income ordinances, so landlords should check local rules in cities such as Charleston, Columbia, Greenville and Myrtle Beach, which are outside this library's scope.

title: Electronic Notices
bodyText: South Carolina's electronic-transactions law does not apply to a notice required by law about default, eviction or the right to cure under a rental agreement for a person's primary residence. Notices of nonpayment, breach and eviction should therefore be delivered on paper, in hand or by registered or certified mail as the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act describes, even if the lease allows e-mail for other communications.

title: Bounced Checks
bodyText: A South Carolina landlord may charge a service charge of up to $30 when a check, draft or other written order given for rent is dishonored. If the writer does not pay the amount plus the $30 charge within 10 days after a written notice in the statutory form is sent by certified mail to the address on the check, that failure is prima facie evidence of fraudulent intent for a criminal bad-check case. No South Carolina statute sets a fee for a failed electronic or card payment.

title: Lead Hazards
bodyText: Federal lead-based paint disclosure rules apply to rentals built before 1978. In addition, when a child lives in a dwelling where South Carolina's public health department identifies a lead-based hazard, the department posts a notice at the dwelling, notifies the occupant and orders the owner to remediate the hazard within a reasonable time; the owner may appeal the order as a contested case. Once a dwelling has been posted and ordered remediated, you may not rent it or offer it for occupancy by children until the hazards are remediated, and if the hazard comes to light while a family with children already rents it, you may not evict the family for that reason.

title: Squatters and Unlawful Occupants
bodyText: Since 2026-06-30, a South Carolina property owner can remove unlawful occupants of a residential dwelling quickly by filing a verified petition with the clerk of court or chief magistrate; the court issues an ex parte removal order, holds a hearing within 24 hours, and the sheriff or constable enforces it. The procedure is only for people who were never tenants: the petition must state that the property was not leased to anyone and the occupants are not current or former tenants, guests or immediate family. Anyone who was a tenant must be evicted through the ordinary ejectment process. The same law made it a crime to rent out property one does not own or lease, to present a fake lease or deed to stay on property, and, as a felony, for an unlawful occupant to cause $1,000 or more in damage.

title: Selling a Rented Property
bodyText: When South Carolina rental property is sold, the buyer becomes the tenant's landlord under the existing lease by operation of law. A seller who sells in good faith to a bona fide purchaser is relieved of liability for events after written notice of the sale to the tenant, but stays liable for the security deposit unless it is transferred to the buyer and the tenant is notified in writing within a reasonable time. A tenant who pays rent to the former owner before receiving notice of the sale is protected. The owner and agent disclosure must be kept current after a sale or a change of manager, and an outgoing manager is released only after written notice to the tenant.

title: Condominium Conversion
bodyText: If a South Carolina owner records a master deed to convert rental units to condominiums, within 30 days the owner must give each tenant in possession a written notice of the conversion and tenants' rights, the building-condition disclosure, and an offer to sell the tenant's unit on terms at least as favorable as those offered to others. The tenant has 60 days to accept and may stay until the lease expires or for 120 days after the notice (90 days if under age 60), whichever is longer, on unchanged terms; a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy has no fixed expiration, so that tenant may stay at least 120 days (90 if under 60) after the notice. A lease may still be terminated for the tenant's violation of its terms.

title: Towing from Rental Property
bodyText: No South Carolina statute located sets rules for a landlord towing vehicles from a private rental lot. A towing company that tows and stores a vehicle without the owner's knowledge must notify the local police or sheriff within one hour, or it is not entitled to any compensation for the tow and storage. Local ordinances may add rules.

title: What the South Carolina Act Covers
bodyText: The South Carolina Residential Landlord and Tenant Act governs rental agreements for dwelling units in South Carolina, including landlord-owned mobile homes. It does not cover residence in an institution incidental to medical, educational or similar services; occupancy under a contract of sale; fraternal or social organization housing; transient stays in hotels, motels or other accommodations subject to the accommodations sales tax; employee housing conditioned on employment; condominium owners and cooperative proprietary lessees; agricultural premises; timeshares; or charitable or emergency shelters. Property leased solely so the lessee can renovate it is not a dwelling unit. Vacation rentals of fewer than 90 days are governed by the separate Vacation Rental Act, and manufactured home park lots by the Manufactured Home Park Tenancy Act; both are outside this library.

title: Lease Terms South Carolina Voids
bodyText: A South Carolina lease may not make the tenant waive rights or remedies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, authorize a confession of judgment, or require the tenant to agree to excuse or limit the landlord's legal liability or to indemnify the landlord for it. Such terms are unenforceable, and a landlord who deliberately uses a lease containing terms known to be prohibited and tries to enforce them can owe the tenant actual damages plus up to the amount of the security deposit and attorney's fees, or up to three months' rent and fees if the use was malicious. Bona fide liquidated damages for lost rent on early termination are allowed. No agreement may let anyone collect rent without the landlord's duty to maintain the property. A lease may not bar a tenant from displaying one portable, removable United States flag in a respectful manner. A contractual lien on a tenant's household goods is unenforceable. A court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable lease or term.

title: Rules and Regulations
bodyText: A South Carolina landlord may adopt rules on the tenant's use and occupancy, but they bind the tenant only if they promote tenants' convenience, safety or welfare, protect the property from abuse, or fairly distribute services; are reasonably related to that purpose; apply fairly to all tenants; are explicit enough to tell the tenant what to do; do not evade the landlord's duties; and the tenant had notice of them at signing or when adopted. A rule adopted after the lease is signed that substantially modifies the tenant's bargain is not valid against a tenant who objects in writing within 30 days after it is announced, if the tenant was told of the right to object.

title: Utility Accounts
bodyText: Unless otherwise agreed in writing, a South Carolina tenant has sole financial responsibility for gas, electric, water, sewer and garbage service to the rented premises, and the landlord is not liable for the tenant's account. A utility may not require a landlord to guarantee a tenant's charges, or refuse service because the landlord will not, except for buildings of four or more units served by a master meter. If an energy-efficiency meter conservation charge is attached to the account, the landlord must give each new tenant written notice of it.

title: Eviction Record Removal
bodyText: Beginning 2027-01-01, South Carolina eviction filings and records, including cases ended by an eviction order or writ, a settlement, or later payment of the judgment, must be removed from the public index and publicly accessible files seven years after final disposition or filing if no additional filing is recorded.

title: Rent Paid to Nonresident Owners
bodyText: South Carolina requires a person who pays $1,200 or more a year in rent to a nonresident owner for the use of South Carolina property to withhold state income tax from each payment. A tenant who pays rent for the tenant's own home is not required to withhold, and the rule does not apply to residential units when the nonresident owns four or fewer of them, or to a nonresident registered with the Secretary of State or the Department of Revenue. A property manager collecting rent for a nonresident owner of more than four units should check whether withholding applies. If you own through an out-of-state LLC, South Carolina treats owning income-producing real property here as transacting business. The LLC must obtain a certificate of authority from the Secretary of State naming an agent for service of process in South Carolina, and until it has one it may not maintain an action or proceeding in South Carolina, an eviction included. Its leases stay valid, and while it is unregistered it is treated as having appointed the Secretary of State as its agent for service on claims arising from its business here (S.C. Code Ann. §§ 33-44-1002, 33-44-1003(b), 33-44-1008). An out-of-state corporation transacting business here without a certificate of authority may not maintain a proceeding until it gets one, and owes a civil penalty of $10 a day, up to $1,000 a year. For a corporation, owning real property without more is not transacting business, so whether renting it out is depends on the facts; get advice before filing (S.C. Code Ann. §§ 33-15-101, 33-15-102). And wherever you live, you can be sued in South Carolina on a claim arising from your interest in South Carolina real property, with the papers served on you outside the state (S.C. Code Ann. §§ 36-2-803(A)(5), 36-2-806).

title: No Limit on Security Deposit Amount
bodyText: South Carolina does not limit the amount of a security deposit, pet deposit or prepaid rent a landlord may require.

title: No Interest on Security Deposits
bodyText: South Carolina does not require a landlord to pay interest on a security deposit or to hold it in an interest-bearing, separate or escrow account. Brokers and property managers must, however, keep tenant deposits in a trust account.

title: No Late Fee Limit
bodyText: South Carolina sets no cap or grace period for late fees. Late charges are treated as part of the rent. A late fee should be stated in the lease and should be a reasonable estimate of the landlord's loss.

title: No Application Fee Limit
bodyText: South Carolina does not limit rental application or screening fees or require refunds of unused fees.

title: No Rent Increase Notice Rule
bodyText: South Carolina has no statute setting a notice period for raising rent. During a fixed term, rent can change only as the lease allows; a month-to-month rent increase in practice follows the 30-day notice for ending the tenancy. A rent increase after a tenant's protected complaint can be retaliation, except that a landlord of more than four adjoining units may raise rent uniformly.

title: No Source-of-Income Protection
bodyText: South Carolina law does not require landlords to accept housing choice vouchers or other rental assistance and does not protect source of income; it also does not preempt local ordinances on the subject.

title: No Immigration-Status Inquiry Rule
bodyText: South Carolina has no statute requiring or forbidding a landlord to ask about an applicant's immigration or citizenship status. A state crime of harboring or sheltering unlawfully present people requires intent to further unlawful entry or avoid detection and is not a screening duty. Federal fair housing law still bars national-origin discrimination.

title: No Radon Disclosure Rule
bodyText: South Carolina does not require a landlord to test for or disclose radon to tenants. (Leases with an option to purchase a one-to-four-unit home are different: the state property-condition disclosure statement, which asks about radon, must be given before signing; see `edu-lease-option-disclosure-sc`.)

title: No Bed Bug Disclosure Rule
bodyText: South Carolina has no statute requiring a landlord to disclose bed bugs or setting a treatment timeline. Bed bugs fall under the landlord's general duty to keep the property fit and habitable and the tenant's duty to keep the unit clean.

title: No Mold Disclosure Rule
bodyText: South Carolina has no statute requiring a landlord to disclose mold or setting a treatment timeline. (Leases with an option to purchase a one-to-four-unit home are different: the state property-condition disclosure statement, which asks about mold, must be given before signing; see `edu-lease-option-disclosure-sc`.) Mold falls under the landlord's general duty to keep the property fit and habitable and the tenant's duty to keep the unit clean.

title: No Carbon Monoxide Alarm Duty
bodyText: South Carolina has no statute requiring carbon monoxide alarms in rental dwellings. Local building codes may require them in new construction.

title: No Flood Disclosure Rule
bodyText: South Carolina does not require a landlord to tell a tenant about past flooding or flood risk. (Leases with an option to purchase a one-to-four-unit home are different: the state property-condition disclosure statement, which asks about flooding, must be given before signing; see `edu-lease-option-disclosure-sc`.)

title: No Tenant EV Charging Right
bodyText: South Carolina gives tenants no statutory right to install electric-vehicle charging.

title: No General Rent Receipt Duty
bodyText: South Carolina has no general duty to give receipts for rent. The one exception: when a tenant raises defenses in an eviction and pays rent as it comes due under the court's rule, the landlord must give a written receipt for each payment, except payments by check.

title: No Right-to-Call-Police Statute
bodyText: South Carolina has no statute protecting a tenant's right to call police or emergency services or limiting nuisance-based penalties for such calls.

title: No Lease Termination on a Tenant's Death
bodyText: South Carolina has no statute ending a lease or setting a special procedure when a tenant dies. The lease continues as a contract with the tenant's estate, and the landlord should deal with the estate's representative; property left behind is handled under the abandonment and ejectment rules.

title: No Move-In Inspection Rule
bodyText: South Carolina does not require a move-in or move-out inspection, inventory or condition report. A written, signed condition record is still the best evidence in a deposit dispute.

title: No Drug Lab Disclosure Rule
bodyText: South Carolina has no statute requiring a landlord to disclose or decontaminate a former methamphetamine lab before renting. (Leases with an option to purchase a one-to-four-unit home are different: the state property-condition disclosure statement, which asks about methamphetamine production, must be given before signing; see `edu-lease-option-disclosure-sc`.)

title: If You Can't Deliver Possession on Time
bodyText: If you fail to deliver possession as the lease requires, rent abates until you do, and the tenant may either end the lease by at least 5 days' written notice, in which case you return all prepaid rent and security, or demand that you perform, sue for possession against you or anyone wrongfully in possession, and recover damages. If a person's failure to deliver possession is willful and not in good faith, the tenant can recover from that person up to the greater of three months' periodic rent or twice actual damages, plus reasonable attorney's fees. You aren't liable for damages if a previous tenant held over without your consent and you made reasonable efforts to get possession (S.C. Code Ann. § 27-40-620).

title: Domestic Violence by a Co-Tenant: Tenant's Right to End the Lease
bodyText: A protected tenant (a victim of domestic abuse or violence by another tenant on the same lease, documented by a restraining order, order of protection or conviction) may end their future obligations by written notice within 60 days after the incident, with the documentation, effective at least 30 days after you receive it unless you agree to an earlier date (S.C. Code Ann. § 27-40-350). The tenant gives up possession and owes rent and other amounts through that date and any damage they caused, but no early-termination fee; any deposit due is returned at the end of the lease; for a month-to-month or week-to-week lease, which has no fixed end, the statute does not say when that is. Other tenants stay liable for the full rent; if the perpetrator is the only remaining tenant, you may end the lease on 5 days' written notice and recover actual damages from them. You may not require the protected tenant to leave before the 60 days end, except by agreement, or retaliate.

title: Fire or Casualty: The Tenant's Options
bodyText: If fire or casualty substantially impairs normal use and occupancy, the tenant may move out immediately and tell you in writing within 7 days that they are ending the lease, which then ends on the date they moved out; or, if continued occupancy is lawful, vacate the unusable part and pay rent reduced in proportion to the drop in fair-market rental value (S.C. Code Ann. § 27-40-650). Account for rent as of the date of the casualty. If the lease ends, return the recoverable deposit and prepaid rent, unless the tenant caused the fire or casualty, in which case you may withhold them but must still give the itemized written notice.

title: No Just-Cause Eviction Requirement
bodyText: South Carolina has no just-cause or good-cause eviction rule. A landlord may decline to renew a fixed-term lease when it ends, or end a week-to-week or month-to-month tenancy by written notice at least 7 or 30 days before the termination date, without giving a reason, however long the tenant has lived there; the end of the term is itself a ground for ejectment. Situational limits still apply: a landlord may not raise rent above fair-market value, cut essential services or sue for possession in retaliation for a tenant's code complaint to a government agency or a complaint to the landlord about a violation of the Act, and a retaliatory refusal to renew can delay recovery of possession for 75 days; a protected domestic-violence tenant may not be made to leave before 60 days after the incident or be retaliated against for ending the lease; and an owner converting a building to condominiums must give tenants written notice and let them stay until the lease expires or for 120 days (90 if under 60), whichever is longer, except for a lease violation. Paying rent into court lets a tenant keep defending a possession case but does not bar eviction. No statute protects tenants' associations. Fair housing law applies everywhere; federal rules for subsidized housing are not covered here.

title: Which Charges Count as Rent
bodyText: Under South Carolina's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, 'rent' means the payment for use of the property and includes late charges, but excludes security deposits and other charges. So an unpaid late fee is unpaid rent under the Act, while other fees the lease imposes (for example a returned-payment fee or a bill for repairs) are not rent under the Act's definition, whatever the lease calls them. Whether a particular charge, such as pet rent, is payment for use of the property or an 'other charge' is not settled by the statute. This library's default clause says an unpaid late fee alone will not support ending the lease; that is a library choice, not a legal limit.

title: Landlord's Right to Fix a Tenant's Breach
bodyText: If a South Carolina tenant breaks the tenant's statutory upkeep duties in a way that materially affects health and safety, and the problem can be fixed by repair, replacing a damaged item or cleaning, the landlord may give written notice specifying the breach and asking the tenant to fix it within 14 days (or as promptly as conditions require in an emergency). If the tenant does not, the landlord may enter, have the work done in a workmanlike manner, and the tenant must reimburse the cost; the landlord also keeps the Act's other remedies. No lease clause is needed for this right. The statute calls the payment reimbursement, not rent, and the Act's definition of rent excludes charges other than late charges, so whether an unpaid repair bill can support a nonpayment eviction is not settled by the statute. For a health-and-safety breach that repair, replacement or cleaning cannot fix, the landlord may instead end the lease if the tenant does not comply within 14 days after written notice.

title: No Statutory Rule on Blank Spaces in a Lease
bodyText: South Carolina has no statute requiring every blank in a residential lease to be filled in or treating a blank as a breach, and its Unfair Trade Practices Act has no list of banned practices such as leaving blanks to be filled in after signing. Complete every blank before signing anyway: a blank leaves the term unclear, and a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable lease or term. A written lease that one side never signed still takes effect if the landlord accepts rent, or the tenant takes possession and pays rent, without reservation, but for no more than one year.

title: No Statutory Covenant of Quiet Possession
bodyText: No South Carolina statute states a landlord's covenant of quiet possession or quiet enjoyment for residential leases. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act protects the tenant's possession in other ways: it limits landlord entry, bars recovering possession by lockout or by cutting essential services, gives the tenant damages for an unlawful ouster, and requires each tenant to keep guests from disturbing other tenants' peaceful enjoyment. Whether South Carolina courts imply a covenant of quiet enjoyment into a lease is case law not read here.

title: Forms South Carolina Law Supplies
bodyText: South Carolina supplies no statutory lease form. Forms the law does supply: the lease paragraph headed 'IF YOU DO NOT PAY YOUR RENT ON TIME', which, in the statute's words or substantially equivalent ones and in bold, conspicuous type, serves as the nonpayment notice for the whole tenancy; the notice of a dishonored check, sent by certified mail, which must be substantially in the statutory form; and the tenant's affidavit and court order staying an eviction on appeal, which may be substantially in the statutory form. Magistrate court forms (the application for ejectment, the rule to vacate or show cause, the writ of ejectment, the bond to stay execution on appeal, and the 2026 petition and order for removing unlawful occupants) are court forms, not statutes, and are on the Judicial Branch's forms page.

title: No Rule on Tenant Security Cameras or Video Doorbells
bodyText: No South Carolina statute addresses whether a tenant may install security cameras or video doorbells, so the lease controls, including its rules on alterations. General criminal laws on recording and on voyeurism still apply to anyone who records other people.

title: No Rule on Algorithmic Rent-Setting
bodyText: South Carolina has no statute on setting rents with algorithmic pricing software or on landlords sharing rent data. Cities and counties may not regulate the amount of rent for private rental property. Federal antitrust law and South Carolina's Unfair Trade Practices Act still apply.

title: Damage Caused by the Tenant
bodyText:
If a South Carolina tenant, a member of the tenant's family, or someone on the property with the tenant's permission deliberately or negligently causes a condition, the tenant cannot end the lease over it as a landlord breach or use the essential-services remedies for it, and rent paid into court during an eviction case is not reduced for it.

Fire or casualty is different: if a fire or casualty substantially impairs use of the home, the tenant may still move out and end the lease by written notice within 7 days, or stay in the usable part at reduced rent, even if the tenant caused it. The tenant's fault there only lets you keep the security deposit and prepaid rent, and you must still send the itemized written notice.

The tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage the property or knowingly let others do so. You may deduct the damage from the deposit and recover actual damages for the breach. For a health or safety problem that repair, replacement or cleaning can fix, you may do the work after 14 days' written notice (sooner in an emergency) and have the tenant reimburse the cost.

If the lease ends, you have a claim for actual damages, with a duty to mitigate. No statute says whether those damages include rent lost until the term would have ended; the library offers an optional clause (`tenant-caused-damage-sc`) that sets that measure. A lease cannot keep the full rent running while a tenant-caused casualty is repaired, because that would waive the tenant's statutory right to reduced rent.

title: No Waiving the Duty to Keep the Home Fit
bodyText: A South Carolina lease can't waive your statutory duties to keep the home fit and habitable, to follow building and housing codes, to keep common areas safe, to supply running water, hot water and reasonable heat, or to keep the systems and appliances you supply in safe working order. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act bars any lease term in which the tenant gives up rights under the Act, and bars collecting rent without the duty to maintain. Knowingly using a forbidden term carries a money penalty (see `edu-prohibited-lease-terms-sc`). What the law does allow is narrow: a written agreement for a single-family home, or an agreement for other units, can make the tenant do specified repairs or maintenance tasks, but only in good faith and not to evade your duties; outside single-family homes it can't cover work needed to bring the unit up to code (see `tenant-repair-agreement-sc`). No statute lets a tenant accept listed defects in exchange for lower rent.

title: Which Repair Duties a Lease Can Change
bodyText:
Only a few of South Carolina's habitability rules bend by agreement.
- (1) Appliances: appliances in the unit are presumed to be yours to maintain unless the lease specifically excludes them, but no appliance or facility needed for essential services (plumbing and sewer, electricity, gas used for heat, hot water or cooking, running water, hot water and heat) can be excluded (see `appliances-excluded-sc`).
- (2) Hot water and heat: the duty to supply them doesn't apply where the building isn't legally required to have them, or where the unit's own equipment, under the tenant's exclusive control and on a direct utility connection, produces them.
- (3) Repairs and tasks: a single-family home's lease can, in writing and in good faith, make the tenant maintain the facilities and appliances you supply and do specified repairs and tasks; in other units the tenant can agree to specified work only if it isn't needed to meet the building code and doesn't reduce your duties to other tenants (see `tenant-repair-agreement-sc`).

The code-compliance duty itself, fitness for habitation and safe common areas can't be changed. No statute deals with a private well or a home without utility water; running water is still owed.

title: Making the Tenant Responsible for Repairs
bodyText:
South Carolina lets a lease move some repair and maintenance work to the tenant, on conditions that depend on the type of home.

**Single-family home:** the agreement must be in writing, and may cover maintaining the systems and appliances you supply and specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations and remodeling.

**Any other unit:** the tenant may agree to do specified repairs, maintenance, alterations or remodeling only if the work isn't needed to bring the unit up to the building and housing codes and the agreement doesn't reduce your duties to other tenants.

In both cases the agreement must be made in good faith and not to evade your duties. No statute requires a rent reduction or other payment in return, a separate signature, or bold type. The library's optional clause `tenant-repair-agreement-sc` follows these rules; use it rather than a general clause that shifts all repairs.

title: Notices a Lease Can't Shorten
bodyText: A South Carolina lease can't shorten or waive the notices the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act gives the tenant: the 14-day notice to cure a non-rent breach, the 7-day and 30-day notices that end a week-to-week or month-to-month tenancy, and the other notice periods the Act sets, because a tenant can't waive rights under the Act. One notice works differently: for unpaid rent, the lease itself can serve as the written notice of nonpayment if it contains the statutory paragraph headed "IF YOU DO NOT PAY YOUR RENT ON TIME" in conspicuous (bold) type; the tenant then gets no other notice before you file, though the five days after the due date still run. That isn't a waiver; it is the notice the statute allows (see `nonpayment-notice-sc`).

title: Notice for Showings
bodyText:
In South Carolina you must give the tenant at least 24 hours' notice before entering, and enter only at reasonable times, for any purpose other than an emergency, regularly scheduled periodic services written into the lease, or services the tenant asked for. Showing the home to prospective tenants or buyers is a lawful reason to enter, and the tenant can't unreasonably refuse, but it still needs the 24 hours' notice.

A lease can't shorten that period, because a tenant can't waive rights under the Act, so this library does not offer South Carolina the optional shorter-notice showing clause other states use. The tenant can agree to a particular showing on shorter notice when you ask at the time.

Entering unlawfully, or so often that it harasses the tenant, lets the tenant get a court order or end the lease and recover damages and attorney's fees.

title: Deposit Rights a Lease Can't Waive
bodyText: A South Carolina lease can't take away the tenant's deposit rights: deductions only for accrued rent and damage caused by the tenant's breach of their duties, an itemized written notice with any balance within 30 days, and three times the amount wrongfully withheld plus attorney's fees if you don't comply. A clause making the deposit nonrefundable, letting you keep it as a penalty, or giving up the itemized notice would be a waiver of rights under the Act and unenforceable, and knowingly using it risks a penalty. The tenant's duty to give you a forwarding address in writing is part of the statute and can be restated in the lease (see `security-deposit-return-sc`).

title: Rules a South Carolina Lease Can't Change
bodyText: South Carolina's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act says a lease may not make the tenant waive rights or remedies under the Act, authorize a confessed judgment, or excuse or limit your liability under law (or make the tenant indemnify you for it); such terms are unenforceable, and if you deliberately use them and try to enforce them, the tenant can recover actual damages plus up to the deposit (up to three months' rent if malicious) and attorney's fees. In practice, your lease can't change: your repair and code duties; the deposit return rules; the 24-hour entry notice; the 14-day cure notice for non-rent breaches and the five days after the due date for rent; the 7- and 30-day notices for periodic tenancies; the ban on lockouts and utility shutoffs; the tenant's rights after a fire or casualty, a failure to deliver possession, or a domestic-violence termination; the ban on retaliation; and your duty to mitigate. Bona fide liquidated damages for loss of rent on early termination are allowed. Disputed claims can be settled by agreement, and a court may refuse unconscionable terms.

title: No Smoke Drift Law
bodyText: No South Carolina statute deals with secondhand smoke drifting between rental units, requires smoke-free housing, or says whether a lease may make a tenant give up a claim about smoke drift. The Clean Indoor Air Act bans smoking in listed public indoor areas, including elevators, but not in apartments or their hallways generally. Because a lease can't excuse or limit your liability under law, don't use a clause in which the tenant gives up smoke-drift complaints; the library's smoking policy (`smoking-policy`) controls smoking instead, and each tenant must keep guests from disturbing other tenants' peaceful enjoyment.

title: Jury Trials and Lease Jury Waivers
bodyText: In a South Carolina eviction (ejectment) case either the landlord or the tenant may demand a jury trial in magistrate court, and the state constitution says the right of trial by jury shall be preserved inviolate. No statute addresses whether a residential lease may waive a jury in advance. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act bars waivers of rights and remedies under that Act; the ejectment jury right sits in a different chapter, so the statute doesn't settle the question, and whether South Carolina courts enforce a pre-dispute jury waiver in a consumer lease is case law we did not search. Cautious course: don't put a jury waiver in a residential lease; this library offers none.

title: No Confessed Judgments in Leases
bodyText: A South Carolina lease may not authorize anyone to confess judgment against the tenant on a claim arising from the lease. A clause like that is unenforceable, and knowingly using it risks the penalty for prohibited terms. South Carolina's general procedure for a judgment by confession still exists outside leases, but it needs a separate written statement signed and sworn by the debtor after stating the facts and the amount, and it can't be built into the rental agreement.

title: Liability Waivers in South Carolina Leases
bodyText: A South Carolina lease may not make the tenant agree to excuse or limit your liability under law, or to indemnify you for that liability or its costs. Such a clause is unenforceable and knowingly using one risks the penalty for prohibited terms. That is why this library uses South Carolina versions of the storage, parking, renter's insurance and services clauses without a blanket "Landlord is not liable" sentence (`storage-space-ks-oh-ca`, `parking-ks-oh-ca`, `tenants-property-insurance-ks-oh-ca`, `services-utilities-provided-ks-oh`). A clause may still allocate risks the law doesn't put on you, such as requiring renter's insurance for the tenant's own belongings, or make the tenant responsible for damage the tenant causes.

title: Unconscionable Lease Terms
bodyText: South Carolina's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act lets a court refuse to enforce a lease, or any term of it, that it finds unconscionable when made, or limit the term to avoid an unconscionable result; the same applies to a settlement in which a party gives up a claim or right. Before deciding, the court must let both sides present evidence of the setting, purpose and effect of the lease. Every duty under the Act also carries an obligation of good faith. No statute defines unconscionable or lists unconscionable lease terms; that is case law we did not search.

title: Attorney's Fees in South Carolina Landlord-Tenant Cases
bodyText: South Carolina's Act sets attorney's fees case by case rather than leaving them to the lease. You can recover reasonable attorney's fees, if you are represented by an attorney, when the tenant's non-rent breach is wilful or the tenant's nonpayment isn't in good faith; after termination you have a claim for actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees; and you get fees for a bad-faith holdover, a tenant's refusal of lawful access, or a tenant defense or counterclaim that is both without merit and not in good faith, or a retaliation defense without merit. The tenant gets fees for wrongful deposit withholding, your wilful noncompliance, an unlawful lockout or utility shutoff, a wilful failure to deliver possession, unlawful or harassing entry, retaliation, and your knowing use of a prohibited lease term. No statute requires a lease fee clause to be mutual, or caps the amount beyond reasonableness. The shared default clause (`default-by-tenant`) claims fees only as the law allows.

title: No Statute on Collection Fees
bodyText: No South Carolina statute authorizes, caps or bans a lease charge for collecting past-due rent, such as a flat collection fee or a percentage added when you send an account to a collector. What the law does say: attorney's fees are recoverable only on the conditions the Act sets (see `edu-attorney-fees-sc`); you recover actual damages for a breach; and a lease can't make the tenant indemnify you for liability or costs the law puts on you. A fee is not "rent" under the Act unless it is a late charge, so an unpaid collection fee doesn't support a nonpayment eviction. Cautious course: charge only actual, reasonable collection costs you can document, and don't add a flat penalty; whether a South Carolina court would enforce a flat collection fee is case law we did not search.

title: No Statute on Charging for Notices
bodyText: No South Carolina statute authorizes or bans a lease charge for preparing, posting or serving a notice (for example a fee for a late-rent notice or a notice to vacate). The Act requires the notices; it doesn't let you charge for them. A charge like that isn't "rent" (only late charges are), so an unpaid notice fee can't support a nonpayment eviction, and court filing costs are set by the court's fee schedule, not the lease. Cautious course: don't charge for serving a notice the law requires; recover court costs only as the court awards them. Whether a flat fee would be enforced is case law we did not search.

title: Charges for an Eviction
bodyText: No South Carolina statute bans or authorizes a lease clause that charges the tenant a fee or penalty for being evicted. Court costs follow the court's fee schedule: magistrates charge a fee for proceedings by a landlord against a tenant (including notices to quit, eviction orders and recovery of rent) of $20, rising to $40 for proceedings from January 1, 2027. Attorney's fees are recoverable only on the conditions the Act sets (see `edu-attorney-fees-sc`). Cautious course: don't add an eviction fee or penalty to the lease; claim the court costs and fees the court awards, and your actual damages.

title: Liquidated Damages for Early Termination
bodyText: South Carolina's ban on prohibited lease terms expressly doesn't invalidate bona fide liquidated damages provisions that set the amount of damages for loss of rent when a lease ends early. That is the basis for the library's early-termination fee (`early-termination-ks`), which applies only to fixed-term leases. The statute speaks only of loss of rent from premature termination; whether a court treats a particular figure as a bona fide estimate rather than a penalty, and whether other fixed charges for breach are enforceable, is case law. Keep the figure a reasonable estimate of lost rent.

title: Casualty and Re-Renting Rules Are Not Waivable
bodyText: South Carolina's fire-or-casualty rule (the tenant may move out and end the lease, or pay reduced rent for the usable part) and the duty to mitigate damages (including your duty to make reasonable efforts to re-rent an abandoned unit) are rules of the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. A lease may not make the tenant waive rights or remedies under the Act, so a clause keeping full rent running after a casualty, or saying you have no duty to re-rent, is unenforceable. The Act's duty to mitigate binds whichever party is harmed, you included. See `edu-casualty-termination-sc` and `edu-abandonment-and-mitigation-sc`.

title: Accepting Rent After a Default
bodyText: South Carolina answers this question only for the period after you file. Once the magistrate issues the rule to vacate or show cause, rent keeps accruing at the same rate while the tenant stays, and accepting any rent, whether it accrued before or after the rule, doesn't waive your right to eject the tenant or renew or extend the tenancy; the parties' rights stay as they were when the rule issued. Before filing (after a default, a notice to cure or a termination notice), no statute says whether accepting rent waives the breach or the notice; that is case law we did not search. The only other statutory rule on accepting rent concerns an unsigned lease: if you accept rent without reservation under a written lease the tenant signed and you didn't, the lease takes effect as if you had signed it. Cautious course: before filing, accept payment only with a written reservation that it doesn't waive the default or the notice, and don't accept rent for a period after the termination date unless you mean to continue the tenancy.

title: Penalty for Using Forbidden Lease Terms
bodyText: If you deliberately use a lease containing terms you know South Carolina forbids (a tenant waiver of rights under the Act, a confessed judgment, or an exculpation or indemnity clause) and try to enforce them, the tenant can recover actual damages plus up to the amount of the security deposit and reasonable attorney's fees. If you do so maliciously, the cap rises to three months' periodic rent plus reasonable attorney's fees. The forbidden term itself is unenforceable either way. No later section of the Act sets a different penalty for its own forbidden terms. Using this library's South Carolina rows keeps you clear of it.

title: Abandonment and Re-Renting
bodyText:
In South Carolina a tenant's unexplained absence for 15 days after a rent default counts as abandonment, and abandonment is immediate if the tenant also voluntarily cut off the utilities.

Once a tenant abandons, you must make reasonable efforts to re-rent at a fair rent. If you re-rent for a term starting before the old lease ends, the old lease ends when the new tenancy starts, and you keep your claim for the old tenant's breach. If you don't make reasonable efforts, or you accept the abandonment as a surrender, the lease is treated as ended by you on the date you learned of the abandonment. For a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy, the term for this purpose is one month or one week.

Every party harmed has a duty to mitigate, and after termination you have a claim for rent, actual damages and attorney's fees. Left-behind property follows `abandoned-property-sc`.

title: Tenant Remedies When You Break the Lease
bodyText: If you materially fail to comply with the lease, or fail to meet your repair duties in a way that materially affects health and safety, a South Carolina tenant may give you written notice that the lease will end in at least 14 days unless you fix it; if you fix it in time (or start within 14 days and finish in good faith, for a problem not affecting health and safety), the lease doesn't end. The tenant can't end the lease over a condition the tenant or their household or guests caused. The tenant may also sue for actual damages and an injunction (with attorney's fees if you acted wilfully), and if the lease ends you must return the recoverable deposit. Separate remedies cover essential services (`edu-tenant-repair-remedies-sc`), failure to deliver possession (`edu-possession-delay-sc`), fire or casualty (`edu-casualty-termination-sc`), unlawful lockout or utility shutoff (three months' rent or twice actual damages, `edu-self-help-eviction-sc`), unlawful entry and retaliation.

title: Your Remedies When a Tenant Breaks the Lease
bodyText: When a South Carolina tenant breaks the lease, your remedies are set by the Act. Unpaid rent: you may end the lease if rent stays unpaid five days after the due date and you have given written notice (once per lease term, or in the lease itself, `nonpayment-notice-sc`). Other breaches: a written notice ending the lease at least 14 days after receipt, which the tenant can stop by curing a remediable breach in time (`default-by-tenant`); illegal activity goes on the five-day track. Health and safety breaches you can fix by repair, replacement or cleaning: after 14 days' notice you may do the work and bill the tenant (`edu-landlord-self-cure-sc`). After termination you have a right to possession and to rent, plus a separate claim for actual damages and attorney's fees; you must mitigate. You recover possession only through the magistrate or circuit court, never by lockout. Money claims can be brought in magistrate court (within its limit) or circuit court; collection by distress needs a magistrate's warrant after a hearing (`edu-landlord-lien-sc`).

title: Tenant Remedies for Repairs
bodyText: South Carolina gives tenants these repair remedies, and no others: (1) a written 14-day notice to fix a breach that materially affects health and safety, after which the lease ends if you don't (`edu-landlord-breach-remedy-sc`); (2) for a negligent or wilful failure to supply essential services (heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas, plumbing and sewer), after written notice, the tenant may buy reasonable amounts of the service and deduct the actual cost from rent, or recover damages for the reduced rental value plus attorney's fees; (3) damages and an injunction; and (4) the right to raise your breach as a defense in a nonpayment case, if you had notice in time. The law expressly does not let a tenant make repairs and deduct the cost from rent, and a mechanic's lien for repairs the tenant orders without your consent is unenforceable. No remedy applies to a condition the tenant or their guests caused. There is no rent escrow except the rent a tenant pays into court while defending an eviction (`edu-rent-into-court-counterclaim-sc`).

title: Rent Comes with the Duty to Maintain
bodyText: In South Carolina no lease, assignment, deed, trust deed, mortgage or security instrument may let anyone receive the rent without also carrying the duty to keep the home up to the Act's maintenance standards. So a lender, buyer or assignee who collects rent takes on those duties, and a lease can't split the right to rent from the duty to repair.

title: Rent Paid Into Court During an Eviction
bodyText: When you sue for possession and a South Carolina tenant raises defenses or counterclaims, the tenant must keep paying you the rent that falls due after the rule to vacate or show cause is issued (you give a written receipt unless the tenant pays by check), and must pay the rent allegedly owed before the rule, or show a receipt or cancelled check proving it was paid. If you disagree about the amount, the court holds an early hearing and decides it; where the dispute is about your breach, the rent is the fair-market rental value, never reduced for a condition the tenant caused. A tenant who doesn't comply gets a warrant of ejectment. In a nonpayment case the tenant may counterclaim for any amount recoverable under the lease or the Act; a defense or counterclaim without merit and not in good faith earns you attorney's fees. The tenant gives up a repair defense if you had no notice in time.

title: Landlord Liens and Distress for Rent
bodyText: A South Carolina lease can't create an enforceable lien or security interest for you in the tenant's household goods. You may collect unpaid rent by distress (seizing the tenant's property on the premises) only through the magistrate: you file an affidavit of the rent due, the tenant is served with notice of a predistress hearing at least five days later, and the magistrate issues a distress warrant only after finding your right valid. Clothing and food, bedsteads, bedding and cooking utensils, and genuine third-party property are exempt, and the tenant may raise defenses under the Act and claim the general exemptions from attachment. Never take or hold the tenant's belongings yourself.

title: When a Repair Problem Is Serious Enough
bodyText: South Carolina ties most tenant remedies to how serious the problem is. The tenant may end the lease only for a material breach of the lease, or for a failure of your repair duties that materially affects health and safety or the physical condition of the property. The essential-services remedies require that you were negligent or wilful in failing to supply heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or plumbing. And a tenant who uses your repair failure as a defense in a nonpayment case is treated as having waived it if you had no notice in time: for non-essential services, 14 days before rent was due; for essential services, enough notice before rent was due to make emergency repairs. No statute lists which defects are material; that is decided case by case.

title: No Habitability Presumptions
bodyText: South Carolina's Act sets no presumption that a home is or isn't habitable, and no presumption that a defect is your fault or the tenant's. The Act's only presumptions in this area are that appliances present in the unit are supplied by you unless the lease specifically excludes them, and that a uniform rent increase by a landlord of more than four adjoining units isn't presumed retaliatory. Each side proves its case on the facts; keep move-in condition records and written repair requests and responses.

title: No Required Habitability Statement in the Lease
bodyText: No South Carolina statute requires the lease itself to state that you will deliver or keep the home fit to live in. The duties apply whatever the lease says: at the start of the term you must deliver possession in compliance with the lease and your maintenance duties, and you must keep the home fit and habitable throughout. The library's landlord maintenance clause (`landlord-maintenance`) describes them; no extra statement is required.

title: Grounds for Eviction and the Right to Cure
bodyText:
South Carolina has two notice tracks.

**Rent:** if rent is unpaid when due and the tenant doesn't pay within five days, you may end the lease after written notice of nonpayment and your intention to terminate; one notice satisfies the duty for the whole lease term, and the lease itself can be that notice (`nonpayment-notice-sc`).

**Other breaches:** give written notice describing the breach and that the lease ends on a date at least 14 days after the tenant receives it; the lease doesn't end if the tenant fixes a remediable breach in time, or starts within 14 days and pursues it in good faith to completion within a reasonable time.

Illegal activity on the premises goes on the five-day track, with no 14-day cure on the better reading (the 14-day provision lists the illegal-activity duty among the breaches it excludes; how courts read the overlap is case law, so state the illegal activity in a written notice giving at least five days); a breach that can't be remedied ends the lease on the 14-day notice.

Health-and-safety breaches have their own track: 14 days after written notice, or as promptly as conditions require in an emergency.

A lease can't shorten these periods. In court, the grounds for ejectment are nonpayment, the end of the term and violation of the lease.

title: The Tenant's Duties Under South Carolina Law
What South Carolina Habitability Law Does Not Contain
bodyText: South Carolina's habitability law (the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act's repair duties and tenant remedies) is complete in itself, but some rules found elsewhere are missing. We found no South Carolina statute that: (1) lets a tenant repair and deduct (the Act expressly says it doesn't, though after written notice a tenant may buy reasonable amounts of essential services you negligently or wilfully fail to provide and deduct their actual and reasonable cost from rent); (2) lets a tenant withhold rent or pay it into an escrow account outside an eviction case (rent keeps being paid to you while the tenant defends a possession case, and on appeal under the tenant's affidavit, where a judge may direct it into escrow while a dispute over the amount or due date is pending); (3) sets specific heating temperatures, repair deadlines other than the Act's 14-day notices and the 15-day deadline to repair or replace a deficient smoke detector after the tenant's written notice (`smoke-detectors-sc`), or a list of material defects; (4) presumes a unit habitable or not (`edu-no-habitability-presumption-sc`); (5) requires a habitability statement in the lease (`edu-no-habitability-statement-rule-sc`); or (6) requires a move-in inspection (`edu-no-move-in-inspection-rule-sc`). Local housing codes may set more detailed standards, and the Act makes you comply with them where they affect health and safety.

title: Keeping Abuse Information Confidential
bodyText: No South Carolina statute makes a private landlord keep confidential what a tenant tells you about domestic violence or abuse, or the documents a protected tenant gives you to end a lease early (a restraining order, an order of protection or evidence of a conviction). South Carolina's victim address confidentiality program, run by the Attorney General, lets a certified victim use a designated address; state and local agencies and the courts must use only that address once the person shows certification, and the Attorney General is the participant's agent for service of process. It doesn't bind private landlords directly, but expect court papers for a participant to use the designated address. If your unit is in a federal covered housing program (public housing, Section 8 vouchers, tax-credit housing and others), the federal Violence Against Women Act requires you to keep information about a tenant's victim status confidential, out of any shared database, and to disclose it only with written consent, when needed in an eviction under that law, or when other law requires. Cautious course for every landlord: keep these documents in a separate confidential file and never tell the abuser or other tenants where the victim lives or why they left.

title: Deposit After a Domestic-Violence Termination
bodyText: When a protected tenant ends their lease obligations early under South Carolina's 2026 domestic-violence law, you don't have to return any deposit until the end of the lease, and then only if it is due under the lease. The statute doesn't say whether that waits for the other tenants to move out; because the cotenants stay liable for the full rent for the rest of the term, the lease (and its deposit) normally continues until the term ends. The protected tenant remains liable for damage they caused before termination. For a month-to-month or week-to-week lease the statute doesn't say when the "end of the lease" is (see `edu-dv-lease-termination-sc`); cautious course: treat it as the date the tenancy ends for all tenants, and then follow the ordinary 30-day itemized return (`security-deposit-return-sc`).

title: Domestic Violence and Eviction
bodyText: South Carolina's protection for tenants who are victims of domestic violence is narrow. Under the 2026 law, where the victim and the abuser are both on the same lease and the abuse is documented by a restraining order, an order of protection or a conviction, you may not require or force the victim to leave before 60 days after the incident (unless you agree on an earlier date), you may not retaliate against a victim who ends the lease early, and if the abuser is left as the only tenant you may end the lease on 5 days' written notice and recover actual damages from the abuser. A landlord who relies in good faith on the victim's documents isn't liable for ending or modifying the lease. A family court order of protection can give the victim temporary possession of a jointly leased home to the exclusion of the abuser, where the abuser has a duty to support the victim or children. We found no South Carolina statute that otherwise bars evicting a tenant because they are a victim, or protects a tenant who calls the police. In federal covered housing (public housing, Section 8, tax-credit housing and others), the Violence Against Women Act bars denying or evicting a tenant because they are a victim, doesn't treat the abuse as a lease violation by the victim, and lets you split the lease to remove only the abuser.

title: Lock Changes for Domestic-Violence Victims
bodyText: South Carolina has no statute giving a domestic-violence victim the right to have the locks changed, and the Act says a tenant may not change the locks without your permission. What to do in practice: if a tenant gives you a court order that grants them possession of the home to the exclusion of another person (a family court order of protection can do this), honor it, don't give the excluded person a key, and change or rekey the locks promptly at the tenant's request. Without such an order, don't lock out a person who is a tenant on the lease, even at the victim's request: removing or excluding a tenant without a court order is an unlawful ouster that costs you three months' rent or twice the actual damages, plus attorney's fees. A victim who is on the same lease as the abuser can also end their own obligations early (see `edu-dv-lease-termination-sc`).

title: Where South Carolina Abuse Laws Are Found
bodyText: South Carolina's landlord-tenant domestic-violence rule (enacted in 2026) defines a qualifying incident by pointing to two chapters, and both are current and where the rule says: the Protection from Domestic Abuse Act (Title 20, Chapter 4), under which the family court issues orders of protection, and the criminal domestic violence chapter (Title 16, Chapter 25). Both define abuse or domestic violence between household members: spouses and former spouses, people with a child in common, and a man and a woman who live or lived together. The Code flags those household-member definitions with a validity note citing a 2017 South Carolina Supreme Court decision; whether they now reach other couples is case law we did not search. Restraining orders for harassment or stalking are issued under a different article (Title 16, Chapter 3, Article 17); such an order documents a qualifying incident only where the conduct is domestic abuse or violence as those two chapters define it.

title: Documents for a Domestic-Violence Termination
bodyText: South Carolina has one landlord-tenant domestic-violence provision (early termination by a protected tenant), so there is one document list: a restraining order, an order of protection, or the abuser's conviction for the domestic violence or abuse. The tenant's written notice must come within 60 days after the documented incident and be accompanied by that documentation; the termination takes effect at least 30 days after you receive the notice, unless you agree in writing to an earlier date. The statute runs the 60 days from the date of the qualifying incident, not from the date of the order or conviction, and doesn't say what happens when an order is issued more than 60 days after the incident. Cautious course: accept a notice given within 60 days after the order or conviction that documents the incident, since you are protected when you rely in good faith on the tenant's documents. A police report or a letter from an advocate is not on the list. The rule applies only where the victim and the abuser are both on the lease for the same property.

title: No Pre-Set Deduction Charges
bodyText: No South Carolina statute lets a lease fix deposit deductions in advance (a set cleaning, carpet or rekeying charge), and none bars a lease from listing typical costs. The deposit statute lets you keep only accrued rent and the damages you actually suffered from the tenant's failure to meet their duties, which include complying with the lease, itemized in a written notice. So a schedule in the lease works as notice of what things usually cost, but deduct what you actually and reasonably spend (keep invoices), not the scheduled figure. Charging a fixed amount whatever the actual cost risks being treated as a forfeiture of deposit rights the tenant can't waive.

title: Unclaimed Deposit Refunds
bodyText: A deposit refund you can't deliver remains the tenant's money. South Carolina's Uniform Unclaimed Property Act lists security deposits as intangible property and makes anyone holding property belonging to another, or owing it, a holder. A deposit refund that stays unclaimed for more than five years after it became payable is presumed abandoned. The holder must then report it to the State Treasurer (the administrator) before November 1 each year, as of the preceding June 30, after sending the owner a written notice at the last known address 120 days or less before the report if the amount is $50 or more and the address isn't known to be wrong, and must pay it over. Failing to report can cost $100 a day up to $5,000, and failing to pay over can cost 25% of the amount plus interest. No statute lets you keep an unclaimed refund, and a lease clause forfeiting it to you would waive the tenant's deposit rights. Mail the itemized notice and any refund to the forwarding address (or the last known address) within 30 days, and keep uncashed refunds on your books.

title: No Deposit Installment Right
bodyText: South Carolina doesn't give tenants a right to pay the security deposit in installments, and doesn't regulate an installment plan you choose to offer. If you allow one, write the schedule into the lease; money paid toward the deposit is still a security deposit held in trust and returned under the usual 30-day rule.

title: Deposits and Last Month's Rent
bodyText: No South Carolina statute deals with last month's rent: it doesn't stop a tenant from asking you to apply the deposit to the final month, and doesn't require you to. Money collected in advance as "last month's rent" is prepaid rent, which the deposit statute treats like a security deposit at the end of the tenancy: return what isn't used, with the itemized notice, within 30 days, or face three times the amount wrongfully withheld plus attorney's fees. Unless the lease says otherwise, the deposit secures the whole lease, so a tenant who skips the last month's rent is still in default; say in the lease whether the deposit may be applied to rent.

title: Conditions on Getting the Deposit Back
bodyText: South Carolina doesn't let you make the deposit refund depend on the tenant giving advance notice of moving out, returning keys by a deadline, or cleaning to a set standard. The statute's only condition on the tenant is a written forwarding address: if the tenant doesn't give one and you had no notice of where they went, they can't claim the statutory damages as long as you mailed the notice and refund to the last known address. Your 30 days run from the later of the end of the tenancy and delivery of possession, or the tenant's demand. A lease can require notice before moving out of a periodic tenancy (that's the 7- or 30-day notice) and charge for real loss, such as unpaid rent or rekeying a lock the tenant didn't return, but not forfeit the deposit as a penalty.

title: No Special Procedure for Deposit Disputes
bodyText: South Carolina has no fast-track or special court procedure for deposit disputes. A tenant who disputes deductions sues in magistrate court (within its money limit) or circuit court, both of which hear claims under the Act, and the remedy for a wrongful withholding is three times the amount wrongfully withheld plus reasonable attorney's fees. Your protection is the paperwork: a timely itemized notice, receipts for repairs, and move-in and move-out records.

title: Fees Instead of a Deposit
bodyText: No South Carolina statute regulates a fee charged in place of a security deposit (a deposit-alternative or surety program), requires you to offer a deposit instead, or limits reporting an unpaid damage claim. What the statute does say: any money from the tenant held in trust to secure the tenant's performance is a security deposit, whatever the lease calls it, and must be returned under the 30-day rule; a true nonrefundable fee that buys a product (such as a surety bond) isn't a deposit. Cautious course: offer a deposit as an alternative, describe in the lease exactly what the fee buys, and say in writing that it doesn't relieve the tenant of liability for damage if that is the case.

title: No Fee-Transparency Law
bodyText:
South Carolina has no rental fee-transparency or all-in pricing law: no rule that rent and mandatory fees appear as one total, that fees go on the lease's first page, or that ads show the full price. The general Unfair Trade Practices Act bans unfair or deceptive acts in trade or commerce, which is defined to include services and real property; whether it reaches a particular landlord's fee practice is case law.

Cautious course: list every fee in the lease (the library's `fees-and-charges-vi` clause does this) and don't charge any fee the lease doesn't state.

title: Fees for Services You Don't Provide
bodyText: No South Carolina statute specifically bars charging a residential tenant for a service you don't provide. The nearest rule is in the Manufactured Home Park Tenancy Act, which bars a park owner from starting to charge a user fee during the rental agreement for a service or amenity that was included in the lot rent, unless the rent goes down to match. For ordinary rentals, a fee for a service never delivered is hard to defend in court and can be an unfair practice. Charge only for services you actually provide and describe them in the lease.

title: Holding Deposits Before the Lease
bodyText: No South Carolina statute governs a holding deposit taken before a lease is signed: there is no cap, no deadline for refunding it if you or the applicant back out, and no rule that it counts toward the security deposit. Once the lease is signed, money you keep to secure the tenant's performance is a security deposit. If a licensed broker or property manager takes the money, it is a trust fund that must go into the firm's trust account within 48 hours (business days) after the lease is signed (checks) or after receipt (cash or certified funds). Cautious course: put the terms in writing: what the money holds, when it becomes the first rent or the deposit, and when it is refunded or kept.

title: No Separate Notice for Nonrefundable Fees
bodyText: South Carolina doesn't require a separate written notice for a nonrefundable fee in an ordinary residential lease. (Vacation rental agreements must state the terms of advance payments, which may be nonrefundable.) What matters is substance: money held in trust to secure performance is a security deposit and must be returned under the statute even if the lease calls it nonrefundable. If you charge a true nonrefundable fee (for example a pet fee or a cleaning fee), name it and its amount in the lease, as the library's `nonrefundable-fees-wv` clause does.

title: Pet Deposits, Fees and Pet Rent
bodyText: South Carolina doesn't regulate pet deposits, pet fees or pet rent and sets no cap (see `edu-no-deposit-cap-sc`).
