A refundable pet deposit held to secure the tenant's performance fits the Act's definition of a security deposit, so return it under the same 30-day itemized rule; licensed brokers and property managers must hold pet deposits in their trust account. A nonrefundable pet fee should be named as such in the lease (`nonrefundable-fees-wv`). Whether monthly pet rent is "rent" (supporting a nonpayment eviction) or an "other charge" isn't settled by the statute (see `edu-fees-as-rent-sc`). Assistance animals aren't pets, and fees for them are governed by fair-housing law.

title: How a Deposit Must Be Held
bodyText: A South Carolina landlord holds the security deposit in trust for the tenant, but the Act doesn't say where: there is no separate-account, escrow, bond or interest requirement, and no notice of where it's held (see `edu-no-deposit-interest-sc`). The rules are stricter for a licensed broker-in-charge or property manager-in-charge: deposits must go into a demand-deposit trust or escrow account at an insured institution authorized in South Carolina, within 48 hours (excluding weekends and bank holidays) after receipt for cash or certified funds, or after the lease is signed for checks, and stay there until the lease ends. The account may bear interest, and the broker may keep the interest only if the owners of the funds were told they own it and gave it up in a written agreement, in conspicuous language if it is a preprinted form.

title: Deposits When the Property Is Sold
bodyText: When you sell a rental in South Carolina in a good-faith sale to a bona fide purchaser, you're released from the lease and the Act for events after you give the tenant written notice of the sale, but you stay liable for the tenant's deposit unless you transfer the deposit to the buyer and the tenant is notified in writing a reasonable time after the sale; then the buyer is liable for it. Whoever holds the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends is bound by the deposit rules. A new owner or manager must also keep the owner-and-agent disclosure current. A manager whose management ends is released for later events after written notice to the tenant.

title: What Happens If You Mishandle the Deposit
bodyText:
If you don't return a South Carolina tenant's deposit or prepaid rent with the required itemized notice within 30 days, the tenant may recover three times the amount wrongfully withheld plus reasonable attorney's fees. The tenant loses that remedy only if they never gave you a written forwarding address and you had no notice of their whereabouts and mailed the notice and refund to the last known address.

If you rent more than four adjoining units, use different standards to set deposits, and didn't post or give the standards before signing, you can't deduct damages from the part of the tenant's deposit above the lowest deposit for a comparable unit.

A lease that makes the tenant waive these rights is unenforceable, and knowingly using one can cost up to the deposit (or three months' rent if malicious) plus fees. Either side can still sue for other damages.

title: South Carolina's Money Limits at a Glance
bodyText: South Carolina sets almost no money caps on residential rentals. No cap on: the security deposit, pet deposit or prepaid rent (`edu-no-deposit-cap-sc`); late fees, and no grace period (`edu-no-late-fee-cap-sc`); application fees (`edu-no-application-fee-cap-sc`); or rent, and cities and counties may not regulate the amount of rent on private rentals. The figures the law does set: deposits returned within 30 days, with three times the amount wrongfully withheld plus fees as the penalty; an unlawful lockout or utility shutoff costs three months' rent or twice actual damages, whichever is greater, plus fees; deliberately using and trying to enforce a forbidden lease term lets the tenant recover actual damages plus up to the deposit (three months' rent if malicious) and fees; an abandoned tenant's property worth $500 or less may be disposed of; interest on sums due without an agreed rate is 8.75% a year; and the magistrate's fee for a landlord-tenant proceeding is $20, rising to $40 for proceedings from January 1, 2027.

title: No Late-Fee Cap, Including Manufactured Home Parks
bodyText: South Carolina caps late fees for no one: neither the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act nor the Manufactured Home Park Tenancy Act sets a cap, a grace period or a separate penalty for late fees (see `edu-no-late-fee-cap-sc`). Under the Act a late charge is part of the rent. A park's written rental agreement must state the amounts the resident will pay, including security deposits, service fees and installation charges, so put any late fee in it.

title: Late Fees When a Subsidy Pays Part of the Rent
bodyText: No South Carolina statute addresses late fees when a housing authority or other subsidy pays part of the rent, for example barring a late fee when the subsidy payment arrives late. If the unit is in a federal program (such as the Housing Choice Voucher program), the program's own lease addendum and rules govern what you may charge the tenant; otherwise the general rule applies: no late-fee cap, and a late charge is part of the rent. Cautious course: charge a late fee only on the tenant's own share.

title: Utility Deposits
bodyText: No South Carolina statute governs a utility deposit that you collect from a tenant. If you take money to secure the tenant's utility charges owed to you under the lease, it is part of the security deposit (money held in trust to secure the tenant's performance) and is returned with the itemized notice within 30 days. Deposits the utility itself takes are governed by Public Service Commission rules: for example, an electric utility must refund a deposit with interest after two years unless the customer has had repeated 30-day arrears, and a utility deposit left unclaimed for more than a year after service ends is presumed abandoned unclaimed property.

title: Charging for a Tampered Smoke Detector
bodyText: South Carolina lets you charge a tenant the actual cost of repairing or replacing a smoke detector that you find, on inspection or testing, was deliberately tampered with, damaged or destroyed by the tenant or someone the tenant authorized to live there, after notifying the tenant in writing of the finding; you then also have no duty to fix it within the usual 15 days. The law doesn't authorize a flat fee or fine for tampering; charge only the actual cost (see `smoke-detectors-sc`). Damage the tenant causes negligently is recoverable as ordinary damages. South Carolina has no carbon monoxide alarm statute.

title: Accessory Dwelling Units
bodyText: No South Carolina statute deals with accessory dwelling units (a garage apartment, in-law suite or backyard cottage): none requires cities or counties to allow them, bars owner-occupancy conditions, or sets rental terms for them. Whether you may build and rent one is a local zoning question; the state's zoning enabling law leaves the matter to each city's or county's ordinance. Once rented, an ADU is a dwelling unit under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act like any other.

title: No State Limit on Renting in Single-Family Zones
bodyText: No South Carolina statute limits renting a home in a single-family zone unless the owner lives there, or requires owner occupancy for any rental. Local zoning and homeowners' association covenants may restrict rentals; the state bars cities and counties only from regulating the amount of rent.

title: No State Landlord Registration
bodyText: South Carolina has no statewide landlord or rental registration and no rule that an out-of-state owner hire an in-state broker. What the state does require: before the tenancy starts you must give the tenant, in writing, the name and address of an owner or an authorized agent for service of process and notices, and keep it current; a nonresident landlord may designate a South Carolina agent for service by filing with the Secretary of State, and if none is designated, service may be made on the Secretary of State. Anyone who manages rentals for others for pay generally needs a real estate license (an owner's own unlicensed employees may perform limited on-site tasks). Cities and counties may require a business license or rental permit; that is local and not covered here.

title: No Required Landlord Insurance
bodyText: South Carolina doesn't require a residential landlord to carry liability or property insurance, and no state registration asks for proof of it. Insurance is a business choice (a lender or association may require it). One related rule: if your property insurer pays you for damage a tenant caused, the insurer can't sue the tenant for it unless the tenant caused the damage intentionally or in reckless disregard of others' rights.

title: Government Inspections of Rentals
bodyText: South Carolina has no statewide rental inspection or licensing-inspection program. Inspections reach rentals in two ways. (1) Unfit dwellings: a city or county that adopts an unfit-dwelling ordinance may investigate on a petition or on its own motion, hold a hearing, and order the owner to repair or to vacate and close (or demolish) a dwelling unfit for human habitation, posting a placard on a closed building and recovering its costs by a lien. (2) Fire inspectors: a local inspector may enter buildings to inspect them, but a private dwelling only with permission, unless there is probable cause of a fire-law violation or imminent danger to the occupant. No statute lets a lease clause give consent for an inspector to enter on the tenant's behalf; the tenant must consent to entry of their home, or the inspector needs one of the statutory grounds. Your own right to enter to inspect is the 24-hour-notice rule (`landlords-access`).

title: Code Enforcement Without Receivership
bodyText: South Carolina has no statute that lets a court appoint a receiver to collect rents and repair a substandard or nuisance rental. Code enforcement runs through local unfit-dwelling ordinances: after notice and a hearing, the local officer may order you to repair (if repair costs are reasonable in relation to value) or to vacate and close or demolish, may do the work if you don't, and recovers the cost as a lien collectible like municipal taxes. The State Fire Marshal has similar powers over unsafe buildings other than single-family homes, duplexes and one-story rooming houses. Nuisance abatement for drug dealing, prostitution or continuous breach of the peace can close a building for a year (see `edu-nuisance-sc`).

title: No Health-District Rental Rules
bodyText: South Carolina has no health-district rental regulations and no statute requiring you to give tenants copies of health or housing regulations on request or to refer them to a health agency. The habitability standard is the Act's duty to comply with applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety; local housing codes and unfit-dwelling ordinances set the details (see `edu-rental-inspection-sc`).

title: No Good-Cause Eviction Law
bodyText: South Carolina has no good-cause or just-cause eviction law and no notice you must give tenants about one. You may end a week-to-week tenancy on 7 days' written notice or a month-to-month tenancy on 30 days' notice, or decline to renew a fixed term, without stating a reason, as long as the reason isn't retaliation for a code complaint or a complaint to you, or discrimination. Cities and counties may not regulate rent amounts; no statute addresses local just-cause ordinances.

title: Tenant's Offer When Rentals Become Condominiums
bodyText: South Carolina has no general tenant opportunity-to-purchase law, but converting a rental building to condominiums triggers one. Within 30 days after recording the master deed, the owner must give each tenant in possession, in writing, the architect's or engineer's report on the building's condition, a notice of the conversion and the tenants' rights, and an offer to sell the tenant's own unit at a stated price and terms at least as favorable as those offered to outsiders. The tenant has 60 days to accept in writing; for 50 more days (15 if the tenant is under 60) the owner can't offer the unit to anyone else on better terms without first offering them to the tenant for 10 days. The tenant needn't move until the lease ends or 120 days after the notice (90 if under 60), whichever is later, on unchanged terms; missing the notice is a defense to a possession action brought too early, but a lease can still be ended for breach. Notices may be hand delivered or mailed to the apartment.

title: No Exemption Notices
bodyText: Because South Carolina has no rent-limit, just-cause or general tenant opportunity-to-purchase law, there is no exemption scheme and no exemption notice, filing or statement to give tenants. The only tenant purchase right, on a condominium conversion, has no exemptions to claim (see `edu-condo-conversion-tenant-offer-sc`).

title: No Expiring Tenant Laws
bodyText: No South Carolina landlord-tenant statute is on a repeal clock. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (in force since 1986), the domestic-violence termination right added in 2026, the 2026 appeal-bond and unauthorized-occupant changes and the condominium-conversion rules have no sunset or dated repeal clause. Two 2026 changes take effect later rather than expire: the higher magistrate fees from January 1, 2027, and the provisions of 2026 Act No. 214 from that date (see the eviction rows).

title: South Carolina's Required Lease Disclosures
Rules That Depend on How Many Units You Have
bodyText: Most South Carolina size rules turn on the size of the building, not a landlord's total portfolio; the exception is the Fair Housing Law's exemption for a single-family house rented by a private individual owner, which applies only if the owner owns no more than three single-family houses at any one time, counting houses held for the owner or whose rental proceeds the owner shares (and rents without a broker or discriminatory advertising). Four or fewer families, owner living in one unit: the state Fair Housing Law's rental provisions don't apply (federal law, including its ban on discriminatory advertising, may still apply, `edu-fair-housing-sc`). More than four dwelling units on the premises: you must also keep common areas reasonably clean (all landlords must keep them reasonably safe). More than four adjoining dwelling units on the premises: you must post or give the deposit standards if you use different ones (`security-deposit-standards-sc`), and a uniform rent increase isn't presumed retaliatory. Both conditions of the deposit rule (more than four adjoining units and different standards) must be met for it to apply. Four or more residential units on a master meter or single connection: the utility-account rules (tenant alone responsible, no landlord guarantee) don't apply (`edu-utilities-sc`). Single-family residence: a written good-faith agreement can shift to the tenant the duty to maintain facilities and appliances, plus specified repairs and maintenance (`tenant-repair-agreement-sc`); in any other unit the tenant can take on only specified repairs or maintenance, not work needed to meet the housing code, and without reducing your duties to other tenants. There is no small-landlord exemption from the Act.

title: Collecting Rent for a Unit with Defects
bodyText: No South Carolina statute bars you from demanding or collecting rent because the unit has defects, but defects limit what you can recover. A tenant sued for possession for nonpayment may raise your breach of the lease or the Act as a defense and counterclaim, if you had notice in time (14 days before rent was due for non-essential services; enough time for emergency repairs for essential services). While the case is pending the tenant keeps paying rent to you; if you disagree about the amount because of your alleged breach, the court sets it at the fair-market rental value at the time of the hearing. Essential-services failures let the tenant buy the service and deduct its cost, or recover the reduced rental value.

title: Rent After a Closing Order
bodyText: No South Carolina statute expressly bars collecting rent after a dwelling is condemned or ordered vacated. But once a local officer orders a dwelling vacated and closed as unfit, the placard says its use or occupation for human habitation is prohibited and unlawful, so you can't lawfully keep renting it, and the tenant has your breach of the duty to keep the home fit and habitable as grounds to end the lease and claim damages. A fire or casualty that makes the unit unusable lets the tenant move out and end the lease, with rent apportioned. Cautious course: stop charging rent from the date of a vacate order, and return prepaid rent and the recoverable deposit.

title: No Duty to Disclose Code Orders
bodyText: We found no South Carolina statute that requires a residential landlord to tell a tenant or applicant about an outstanding inspection order, code violation or closing order. An unfit-dwelling order is served on the owner and parties in interest, and a closed building is placarded; renting a placarded dwelling is unlawful. Hiding a known serious defect can still support claims under general law, which we did not search.

title: Voucher Inspections
bodyText: South Carolina has no statute on a subsidized tenant's refusal of a housing-program inspection, and none barring you from declining a voucher tenancy or ending one because of the program's inspection requirements; the state fair-housing law doesn't list source of income. Federal program rules (the Housing Choice Voucher contract and lease addendum) govern inspections in those tenancies, and fair-housing law bars treating a voucher holder differently because of a protected characteristic.

title: Nuisance Abatement and Rentals
bodyText: South Carolina's nuisance-abatement law makes anyone who owns, leases or occupies a building used for lewdness, prostitution, repeated unlawful possession or sale of controlled substances, or continuous breach of the peace guilty of a nuisance. The Attorney General, the solicitor or a citizen may sue to enjoin it. If the nuisance is established, the court orders the fixtures and movable property used in it sold and the building closed for any use for a year, unless the owner pays the costs and posts a bond for the property's full value conditioned on abating the nuisance. No proceeding may be brought against the owner of the real estate without 10 days' written notice from the prosecuting attorney first. There is no nuisance receivership and no statute giving the owner a special motion to cancel the lease; use the Act's remedies (illegal activity on the premises is a five-day ground, see `edu-cure-and-eviction-grounds-sc`). Keeping a drug house is also a crime.

title: Disclosure Statement for a Lease With an Option to Buy
bodyText: If you lease a home of one to four units with an option to purchase, South Carolina's Residential Property Condition Disclosure Act applies. Before the lease-option is signed (or as the contract provides), give the tenant the Real Estate Commission's disclosure statement. It covers, among other things, the water and sewer systems, structure and roof, mechanical systems, wood-destroying insects, zoning and covenants, lead-based paint, asbestos, radon and other environmental contamination, existing leases, any meter conservation charge and any homeowners association; for each item you may state your actual knowledge or make no representation. Skipping the form doesn't void the contract, but knowingly failing a duty under the Act, or giving a statement you know is false, incomplete or misleading, makes you liable for actual damages and court costs, and the court may award attorney's fees. The parties may agree in writing not to complete the statement.

title: Barring Non-Tenants Under the Trespass Law
bodyText: South Carolina's trespass-after-notice law makes it a misdemeanor to enter the premises of another after being warned not to, or to refuse to leave when asked by the person in possession or that person's agent, without legal cause or good excuse. You are the person in possession of the common areas, so you (or your manager) can warn a non-tenant off them and call the police if the person returns or won't leave. A tenant's own unit is in the tenant's possession: you can't bar a guest the tenant invites into the unit, and a tenant's guest on the way to the unit has a good excuse, so make a bar on a specific person part of the lease rules and enforce it against the tenant under the Act if needed. Since June 30, 2026, a separate fast court procedure removes people who were never tenants from a residential dwelling (see `edu-unauthorized-occupant-removal-sc`); it doesn't limit an officer's power to arrest them for trespass.

title: Evicting for Criminal Activity
bodyText: South Carolina has no separate fast-track eviction for violent crime or drug dealing, but illegal activity is on the short track. Unless otherwise agreed, a tenant must use the unit only as a dwelling and must not conduct or permit illegal activities there; if the tenant does, you may end the lease after written notice, on the same five-day basis as nonpayment (on the cure question, see `edu-cure-and-eviction-grounds-sc`). The case then runs through the ordinary ejectment process (rule to vacate or show cause, 10 days, writ). No statute lets a third party (a prosecutor or tenant group) bring the eviction, makes eviction a landlord duty, or regulates crime-free lease addenda. Separately, a building used for repeated drug sales can be closed as a nuisance (`edu-nuisance-sc`).

title: Criminal Activity in a Rental
Bonds in South Carolina Ejectment Cases
bodyText: South Carolina has no end-of-term possession bond or confessed-judgment bond (a lease can't authorize a confessed judgment at all, `edu-confession-of-judgment-sc`). The bonds that exist are on appeal. A judgment for ejectment can't be stayed, except that a residential tenant who appeals to circuit court may file an affidavit promising to pay the rent the magistrate set as it comes due; once the court accepts it, execution is stayed. If the tenant misses a payment by five days, the stay dissolves on your application, the possession appeal is dismissed and the sheriff may remove the tenant (with notice to the appellate court if you apply to the magistrate). Either side may ask the circuit court to modify the amount or due date. Appeals to the Court of Appeals or Supreme Court need a fresh affidavit. The older ejectment chapter's appeal bond for costs and damages yields to the Act where inconsistent; for a residential tenancy, rely on the rent affidavit.

title: No Hardship Stay of Eviction
bodyText: South Carolina has no hardship stay of eviction. A court may not stay execution of a judgment for ejectment, except on appeal when the tenant files the rent-payment affidavit (see `edu-possession-bond-sc`). The one softening is at the door: when executing the writ, the constable or deputy may use discretion to delay removing ill or elderly tenants. The officer must also give the occupants a copy of the writ and 24 hours to leave voluntarily (posting the writ if no one answers) before a deputy may enter by force. Federal law (the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act) can require a stay for tenants in military service.

title: The Tenant's Belongings After an Eviction
bodyText: South Carolina has no storage, inventory or care duty for a tenant's belongings removed in an eviction. The officer executing the writ removes the occupants; belongings removed in the eviction and placed on a public street or highway are removed by the city or county after 48 hours (excluding weekends and holidays), or earlier in normal trash collection; where the local government doesn't collect such debris, you may dispose of them as trash after 48 hours. Your eviction notice must clearly tell the tenant about this rule. Property left after an abandonment or the end of the lease follows a separate rule: if the tenant removed a substantial part of their property or permanently cut off the utilities and left property worth $500 or less, you may enter and dispose of it; otherwise you must have it removed through the ejectment process (`abandoned-property-sc`). No statute addresses pets left behind or makes it a separate crime to return after a writ; returning after being warned off is trespass.

title: Rent Records and Tenant Data
bodyText: South Carolina doesn't require you to keep a rent ledger, give one on request, or attach one to a nonpayment notice. The record rules that do exist: a tenant who raises defenses in an eviction must pay rent as it comes due and gets a written receipt for each payment unless paying by check (`edu-no-cash-receipt-duty-sc`); licensed brokers and property managers must keep a separate record for each tenant showing rent, due date, deposit and receipts, for at least five years; and from January 1, 2027, eviction filings and records must be removed from the public index seven years after final disposition or filing if nothing more is filed (`edu-eviction-record-removal-sc`). If you keep applicants' or tenants' personal identifying information (such as Social Security numbers or bank account numbers) in computerized or other data, the state breach law requires you to notify affected South Carolina residents of a security breach without unreasonable delay, and you may not publicly display a Social Security number or require it to be sent over an unsecured Internet connection.

title: Who Receives Eviction Papers
bodyText: South Carolina's rule works the other way round: you must disclose in writing, at or before the start of the tenancy, the name and address of an owner or an agent authorized to receive service of process and notices, and keep it current; if a manager fails to disclose, the manager becomes your agent for service. Nothing in the Act lets the lease name a third person to accept eviction papers for the tenant. The rule to vacate or show cause is served on the tenant like a summons, or, after two failed attempts at least 48 hours and 8 hours of the day apart, by posting it with proof of the attempts and mailing it; if the unit has been abandoned for 15 days, by posting alone. A tenant in the state's address confidentiality program has designated the Attorney General as agent for service of process, and courts must use the participant's designated address.

title: Minors as Tenants
bodyText: In South Carolina a person 18 or older has full legal rights and responsibilities, so 18 is the age to sign a lease. No statute says who may be named as a defendant in an ejectment case or bars naming minors. A minor's contract generally can't be enforced against them later unless it is for necessaries or they ratify it in a signed writing after turning 18; whether housing is a necessary is case law we did not search. Cautious course: have an adult sign as tenant (or guarantor) and list minors as occupants, not tenants. The ejectment rule is directed at the tenant, and the writ removes all occupants.

title: No Right to Redeem by Paying
bodyText: South Carolina gives a tenant no statutory right to stop an eviction by paying the rent owed before the hearing or the writ, and no rule that you must take such a payment or that partial payments need special reservation wording. Once you have filed, accepting rent doesn't waive the ejectment (`edu-waiver-by-acceptance-sc`). A tenant who raises defenses must pay the rent into the case as it comes due, and the alleged past rent, or face a warrant of ejectment (`edu-rent-into-court-counterclaim-sc`). Whether you accept a late payment and drop the case is your choice; if you do, say in writing whether the tenancy continues.

title: No Relief From Forfeiture for Late Rent
bodyText: No South Carolina statute lets a tenant who is behind on rent undo the end of the lease, or stop your ejectment case, by paying what's owed before the court rules. If rent isn't paid within five days of the due date after the required notice, you may end the lease and file; the tenant's routes are defenses and counterclaims (paying rent into the case meanwhile), not a statutory cure. See `edu-no-redemption-right-sc`.

title: Late Benefit or Voucher Payments
bodyText: No South Carolina statute requires a continuance or reinstatement when a tenant's rent is late because a government benefit or voucher payment arrived late. The ordinary rules apply: five days after the due date plus the nonpayment notice. In federal voucher tenancies, the program contract and lease addendum govern the housing authority's share, and you generally can't evict the tenant for the authority's failure to pay its share.

title: A Tenant's Bankruptcy
bodyText: No South Carolina statute addresses enforcing a writ of ejectment after a tenant files for bankruptcy. Federal bankruptcy law controls: the filing generally creates an automatic stay of eviction proceedings, with limited exceptions (for example where you already have a judgment for possession before the filing, subject to the tenant's limited cure right). Stop and get advice before continuing a case or having a writ executed after you receive notice of a filing.

title: Landlord Rules Outside the Landlord-Tenant Law
bodyText: Three common outside-the-Act rules, as they stand in South Carolina: (1) Squatters: since June 30, 2026 there is a specific remedy. An owner may petition for an ex parte order removing unlawful occupants (people who were never tenants) from a residential dwelling, with a hearing within 24 hours and enforcement by the sheriff or constable; knowingly renting out property you have no ownership or leasehold interest in, or knowingly presenting a fake lease or deed to stay on property, is a crime, and an unlawful occupant who intentionally damages the dwelling by $1,000 or more commits a felony (`edu-unauthorized-occupant-removal-sc`). (2) Cash rent receipts: no general duty (`edu-no-cash-receipt-duty-sc`). (3) Landlord registration as a precondition to a possession judgment: none at the state level (`edu-no-landlord-registration-rule-sc`).

title: No Lockouts for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: South Carolina doesn't allow a landlord to lock a tenant out for unpaid rent, even with advance notice or a lease clause. You may not recover or take possession by any means, including wilfully interrupting essential services, except after abandonment, surrender, termination or as the Act permits, which means a court ejectment. An unlawful lockout or shutoff lets the tenant recover possession or end the lease and recover three months' rent or twice actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees. A lease clause allowing a lockout would waive the tenant's rights under the Act and be unenforceable. See `edu-self-help-eviction-sc`.

title: Notices That Must Be in Writing
bodyText:
Many South Carolina landlord-tenant notices must be in writing, and a lease can't downgrade them to verbal notice, because a tenant can't waive rights under the Act.

In writing: the owner/agent disclosure; the 14-day notice to cure a breach and the nonpayment notice (or the bold lease paragraph that replaces it); the 7- and 30-day notices ending periodic tenancies; the 14-day health-and-safety notices; the tenant's notices of your breach and of essential-services failures; the tenant's forwarding address and your itemized deposit notice; a protected tenant's domestic-violence termination notice; a tenant's notice of a deficient smoke detector; and your notice of a sale.

The 24-hour notice before entry isn't required by the statute to be written, though writing it (or texting it) gives you proof.

A notice to the tenant is received when handed to them or mailed by registered or certified mail to the address they designated or their last known residence, and proof of such mailing is notice; a notice to you is received when delivered at your place of business or the place you designate.

title: Agreeing on Extra Ways to Give Notice
bodyText: South Carolina's Act has no separate "actual notice" standard and no rule letting (or forbidding) the lease add a way of giving notice, such as a text message. It defines notice instead: you give notice by taking steps reasonably calculated to inform the tenant in the ordinary course, and the tenant receives it when it comes to their attention, when it is handed to them, or when it is mailed by registered or certified mail to the address they designated (or their last known residence). A text or e-mail the tenant actually reads counts, but you carry the proof. The electronic-transactions law doesn't reach required notices of default, eviction or the right to cure for a primary residence, so give those on paper (see `edu-electronic-notices-sc`). Use texts and e-mail for routine messages such as entry notices, and keep the delivery methods the Act names for anything that starts a deadline (see `edu-written-notice-required-sc`).

title: Notice of Proceedings Affecting the Property
bodyText:
No South Carolina statute requires you to tell tenants about a lawsuit, foreclosure, tax sale, condemnation or code-enforcement case affecting the property, and none requires a tenant to pass such papers on to you; the library's `tenant-forward-proceedings-ca` clause, which carries SC, adds that tenant duty by contract.

Two statutes help you: a tenant's attornment to a stranger claiming title (agreeing to hold under them) is void unless made under a court order, with your consent or after a sale, and a buyer of rented property steps into your shoes as landlord (see `edu-sale-of-rented-property-sc`). Some proceedings reach tenants directly: a city's complaint or order against an unfit dwelling is served on the owner and parties in interest and posted on the premises.

Cautious course: tell tenants promptly in writing of any proceeding you know will affect their possession or rent, and who to pay.

title: Entering to Care for a Tenant's Animal
bodyText: No South Carolina statute lets you enter a rental to feed, care for or remove a tenant's animal, and the Act says you have no right of access beyond the ones it lists: emergencies (at any time), regularly scheduled services set out conspicuously in the lease, services the tenant requests, a court order, the repair and abandonment remedies, service of ejectment papers with a law enforcement officer, abandonment or surrender, and entry for inspection, repairs, agreed services or showings on at least 24 hours' notice at reasonable times (which the tenant may not unreasonably refuse). An animal in real distress may be an emergency, but the Act doesn't say so. Cautious course: have the tenant name an emergency contact for their animals, try to reach the tenant and get consent at the time, and if you can't, call law enforcement or county animal control rather than handing a key to a third party. Abandoning an animal without providing food, water and shelter is a crime, and officers and humane-society agents can ask a magistrate for an order to take custody of a neglected animal. If the tenant has abandoned the unit, see `abandoned-property-sc`.

title: No Duty to Provide Alternative Housing
bodyText: South Carolina doesn't require you to provide or pay for substitute housing, a hotel or relocation costs when a unit becomes unusable, whether or not the tenant asks. The tenant's remedies are elsewhere: after a fire or casualty that substantially impairs use, the tenant may move out and end the lease (with written notice within seven days) or, if staying is lawful, stop using the unusable part and pay reduced rent (see `edu-casualty-termination-sc`); if you negligently or wilfully fail to supply essential services, the tenant may give written notice and buy reasonable amounts of the service and deduct the cost, or recover reduced-value damages (`edu-tenant-repair-remedies-sc`). Unlike the model act, South Carolina's version gives no substitute-housing remedy. You may offer the tenant another unit you own; put any move, rent and deposit terms in a signed writing.

title: Asbestos in a Rental
bodyText: South Carolina has no asbestos disclosure, inspection or notice rule for ordinary residential leases. (A lease with an option to purchase a one-to-four-unit home is different: before it is signed, the owner must give the state property-condition disclosure statement, which asks about known asbestos.) What the state does regulate is the work: anyone involved in an asbestos project (inspection, design, air monitoring, management, encapsulation, enclosure, renovation, repair, removal or other disturbance of regulated asbestos-containing material, and demolition of a regulated facility) must get a project license from the Department of Environmental Services before starting, under DES regulations; violations can bring civil penalties of up to $10,000 each. Under those regulations, projects at a private residential building of four or fewer units may be exempt, unless done by a licensed abatement contractor, as part of a larger commercial or public project, across several buildings under one owner, at a building that counts as an installation, or for fire training; larger apartment buildings are regulated facilities. Cautious course: before renovating or demolishing older materials (pipe insulation, floor tile, textured ceilings), have them tested, use a licensed contractor if asbestos is found, keep tenants out of the work area, and tell tenants about known asbestos that the work may disturb.

title: No Duty to Disclose Association Documents
bodyText: No South Carolina statute requires a lease of a condominium or homeowners'-association home to disclose the association's obligations, give the tenant its documents, or name a repair contact. The association documents are public: a homeowners association's governing documents must be recorded in the county to be enforceable, its rules must be re-recorded by January 10 each year after adoption or amendment to stay enforceable, and a condominium's master deed must state any restrictions on leasing units. But your own lease rules bind the tenant only if the tenant had notice of them at signing or when adopted, so if the lease makes the tenant follow the association's rules (`hoa-compliance`), give the tenant a copy of the rules and covenants that affect occupants before signing and any later changes when you get them.

title: Renting a Home in an Association
Automatic Renewal Clauses
bodyText:
No South Carolina statute regulates automatic renewal of a residential lease: no bold-type or opt-in requirement, no reminder notice before the renewal deadline, and no limit on how early you can ask a tenant to commit to renewing. The Act lets the lease set its own term and other terms, so an auto-renewal clause is enforceable as written; the library's optional `automatic-renewal-ks` clause carries SC.

The state's consumer auto-renewal rule (a 30-to-60-day notice before the cancellation deadline) covers consumer service contracts, not leases, and a separate rule bars a broker's property management agreement from auto-renewing unless either side can cancel on 30 days' notice after the original end date.

If the lease doesn't renew and doesn't otherwise provide, a tenant who stays on with your consent becomes month to month (`edu-holdover-remedies-sc`). Refusing to renew in retaliation for a protected complaint is barred (`edu-retaliation-sc`).

title: No Balcony Inspection Rule
bodyText: South Carolina has no periodic inspection requirement for balconies, decks or other exterior elevated elements of rental buildings. Statewide building codes (the International codes the Building Codes Council adopts) govern how balconies and decks are built, including guards on open sides more than 30 inches above the floor or grade below. Codes for existing buildings and property maintenance are adopted, if at all, by each city or county. Your general duties still reach a failing balcony: comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, keep the premises fit and habitable, and keep common areas reasonably safe. Cautious course: have older wood balconies, decks and stairs looked at regularly, fix rot and loose railings promptly, and close an unsafe one until it's repaired.

title: Arbitration Clauses in a South Carolina Lease
bodyText: South Carolina's Uniform Arbitration Act makes a written agreement to arbitrate future disputes enforceable, but only if notice that the contract is subject to arbitration is typed in underlined capital letters, or rubber-stamped prominently, on the first page of the contract; without it, the state act doesn't apply. The act also excludes any claim arising out of personal injury. Nothing in the landlord-tenant law mentions arbitration, and the Act gives magistrate and circuit courts jurisdiction over landlord-tenant claims and keeps the jury right in ejectment. A lease may not make a tenant waive rights or remedies under the Act, and using a term you know is prohibited carries a penalty; whether an arbitration clause is such a waiver is unsettled. The library's arbitration clause doesn't carry SC for these reasons. Cautious course: don't require arbitration; if you use it, cover money claims only, keep possession, deposit and injury claims in court, preserve every statutory remedy, and put the first-page notice on the lease.

title: Marijuana and Hemp in a South Carolina Rental
bodyText:
South Carolina has no medical or adult-use marijuana program and no housing protection for cannabis users. Marijuana is a controlled substance: growing, selling or possessing it is a crime, and a tenant must not conduct or permit illegal activity in the unit, which is a ground to end the lease on the five-day track (`edu-no-expedited-criminal-eviction-sc`).

You may ban smoking, vaping, growing and possessing marijuana anywhere on the property (`cannabis-restrictions-ak`, and the smoking ban in `smoking-policy`).

Two narrow exceptions don't change that: certain low-THC cannabidiol preparations (no more than 0.9% THC and more than 15% cannabidiol) used by people with a physician's certification of severe epilepsy aren't legally "marijuana", and growing hemp requires a state hemp license, so a tenant can't grow it at home without one. If a tenant asks to use a lawful cannabidiol product as a disability accommodation, treat it as a fair-housing request (`edu-fair-housing-sc`).

title: No Certificate of Occupancy Disclosure
bodyText: South Carolina doesn't require you to tell a tenant whether the unit needs or has a certificate of occupancy, and no statute bars collecting rent for a unit without one. Certificates of occupancy are issued by the local building official under the building codes the state adopts, and whether an existing rental needs one (for example after a conversion or major renovation) is a local permitting question. Renting a unit that the building codes say may not be occupied would breach your duty to comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety. Cautious course: confirm with the local building department before renting a newly built, converted or substantially renovated unit, and keep the certificate on file.

title: Children in a Rental
bodyText: South Carolina law doesn't require a lease to say anything about children, but the state Fair Housing Law bars refusing to rent, or setting different terms, because of familial status: a household with a child under 18 living with a parent, legal custodian or their designee, and anyone pregnant or securing custody of a child. Advertising a preference against children is also barred. Housing for older persons (62 and over, or qualifying 55-and-over housing) is exempt from the familial-status rules, and small owner-occupied buildings and some single-family homes rented without a broker are exempt from the rental ban (`edu-fair-housing-sc`). You may set reasonable occupancy standards based on bedroom number and size and the unit's overall size, applied to every occupant regardless of age, and ask on the application about the number, ages and relationships of intended occupants. A lead rule also protects children: once a unit is posted and ordered remediated for a lead hazard, you may not rent it to a household with young children until it's fixed, or evict a family with children for that reason (`edu-lead-hazards-sc`).

title: No Cold-Weather Vacating Notice
bodyText: South Carolina has no statute requiring a tenant to warn you before leaving a unit empty in cold weather, and no freeze-protection rule for rentals. The tenant's general duties apply: use heating and plumbing in a reasonable manner and don't negligently damage the premises. The entry statute helps you here: you may enter at any time in an emergency, and prospective changes in weather that pose a likelihood of danger to the property may be treated as an emergency. If you want notice of long absences and a minimum thermostat setting, put them in the lease; the library's `cold-weather-vacate-notice-wy` clause, which carries SC, does this.

title: Leases of Catawba and Other Special Lands
bodyText: South Carolina has no communal-land regime and no rule that a government officer approve an ordinary residential lease. The one special-land statute is old: a lease of lands vested in the Catawba Indians by state law may run up to 99 years or three lives, and is valid only if signed and sealed by at least four of the head men or chiefs. Under the Catawba settlement, the Reservation is land held in trust by the United States Secretary of the Interior, while the Tribe may lease its non-Reservation lands like anyone else under state law. If you are leasing, or subleasing, land on the Catawba Reservation or other land held in federal trust, federal approval rules may apply; get advice before signing. Leases of land owned by state agencies and universities need agency approval, but that binds the public owner, not private landlords.

title: Liens for a Tenant's Work
bodyText:
South Carolina's mechanics' lien law gives a contractor or supplier a lien on a building and on the owner's interest in the land for work done by agreement with, or by consent of, the owner or someone authorized by the owner. So if you consent to a tenant's alterations, a contractor the tenant hires may argue your consent exposes your property; South Carolina has no notice-of-nonresponsibility procedure, and no statute lets a lease clause keep your interest lien-free.

One rule protects you: a tenant who, without your consent, authorizes repairs and tries to deduct them under the essential-services remedy can't create an enforceable mechanic's lien.

Cautious course: require written consent for any work (`no-alterations`), make consent "between us only", require the tenant to pay contractors and clear any lien (`no-liens-ar`), and get lien waivers for larger jobs.

title: The Unfair Trade Practices Act and Rentals
bodyText: South Carolina's Unfair Trade Practices Act bans unfair or deceptive acts in any trade or commerce, which it defines to include offering and distributing real property. It doesn't mention leases or list landlord practices (such as blank spaces or not giving a copy at signing), and whether and when it reaches a residential landlord is case law we did not search. The Act exempts transactions permitted by another state law, so following the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act is your best defense. If it applies, a tenant who loses money because of a deceptive practice may sue for actual damages, three times damages for a wilful or knowing violation (one you knew or should have known was unlawful), and attorney's fees. One rule clearly reaches rentals: during a declared state of emergency or disaster, or after the Attorney General gives notice of an abnormal market disruption, charging an unconscionable price to rent or lease a dwelling unit in the affected area is unlawful and, if wilful, a misdemeanor (`edu-disaster-duties-sc`).

title: Hurricanes and Other Declared Disasters
bodyText: South Carolina has no statute that ends a tenancy, suspends rent or pauses evictions after a declared hurricane or other disaster. The rules that apply: (1) Price gouging: once the Governor declares a state of emergency (or the President declares a disaster that includes South Carolina, or the Attorney General gives notice of an abnormal market disruption), you may not charge an unconscionable price to rent or lease a dwelling unit in the affected area. A price is presumed unconscionable if it grossly exceeds the average in the 30 days before the declaration and the increase isn't explained by added costs, market trends or the usual seasonal change. Wilful violations are misdemeanors and also unfair trade practices (`edu-consumer-protection-act-sc`). (2) Storm damage: if a fire or casualty substantially impairs use of the unit, the tenant may move out and end the lease, or stay and pay reduced rent for the usable part (`edu-casualty-termination-sc`). (3) Vacation rentals: a tenant must obey a mandatory evacuation order.

title: Housing People Displaced by a Disaster
bodyText: No South Carolina statute lets a tenant house people displaced by a hurricane or other disaster in spite of the lease's guest or occupancy limits, bars you from enforcing those limits after a disaster, or lets the state place evacuees in private rentals; the state's evacuation plans arrange housing through government, not private leases. So the lease's guest and occupancy terms still apply (`guest-policy`, `guest-policy-day-limit`, `permitted-occupants`). Cautious course after a disaster: be flexible, agree in writing to any temporary extra occupants (who and for how long), and don't raise the rent for them during a declared emergency, since an unconscionable rental price in the declared area is unlawful (`edu-disaster-duties-sc`).

title: Defective Drywall
bodyText: South Carolina has no defective (corrosive) drywall disclosure rule for an ordinary residential lease. The one place it comes up is the state property-condition disclosure statement, which an owner must give before signing a sale contract or a lease with an option to purchase a one-to-four-unit home; the Real Estate Commission's form asks about known environmental problems including "corrosion-causing sheetrock". An owner who knowingly gives false, incomplete or misleading information on that statement is liable for actual damages. For a plain lease, defective drywall that causes corrosion, odors or failing wiring falls under your duties to comply with health and safety codes and keep the unit fit and habitable; disclose known problems before signing.

title: Naming Who Makes Repairs
bodyText: No South Carolina statute deals with a landlord-designated repairer, an approved-contractor list or a repair contact, and the Act gives tenants no general right to repair and deduct: the essential-services remedy lets a tenant, after written notice, buy reasonable amounts of an essential service you negligently or wilfully fail to provide and deduct the cost, but expressly doesn't authorize repairs. So you may name a repair contact and require your written approval (naming the contractor and a cost limit) before any repair at your expense. Don't write the clause so broadly that it bars the essential-services remedy, which a lease can't waive (`edu-tenant-repair-remedies-sc`). For single-family homes and specified tasks, a written agreement can put some repairs on the tenant (`tenant-repair-agreement-sc`). The owner-or-agent disclosure gives tenants the address for notices (`landlord-disclosure-sc`).

title: Disability Accommodations and Modifications
bodyText:
Under the South Carolina Fair Housing Law it is discrimination to refuse (1) reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices or services needed to give a person with a disability equal opportunity to use and enjoy the home, or (2) reasonable modifications of the premises, at the tenant's expense, needed for full enjoyment. In a rental you may, where reasonable, condition a modification on the tenant agreeing to restore the interior to its prior condition, reasonable wear and tear excepted (the library's `disability-modification-restoration-mn` clause, which carries SC).

A separate statute gives blind, visually impaired and other physically disabled people full and equal access to housing offered for rent, and a person with an assistance dog full and equal access with no extra charge for the dog (they remain liable for damage it does); it doesn't require you to modify your property or provide a higher degree of care. A room in a single-family home where the occupants rent out no more than one room is outside that statute.

Assistance animals: `assistance-animal-accommodation-sc`.

title: Renting the Same Unit Twice
bodyText: South Carolina has no statute on double letting (renting the same room or unit to two tenants for the same period). If you do, the tenant you can't put in possession on the start date has the Act's remedies: rent abates until you deliver possession, and the tenant may end the lease on at least five days' written notice and get back all prepaid rent and deposit, or insist on the lease, sue for possession and recover actual damages. If the failure is wilful and not in good faith, the tenant can recover up to three months' rent or twice actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees (`edu-possession-delay-sc`). Separately, it is a crime to rent property to someone knowing you have no ownership or leasehold interest in it. Keep one booking record per unit and don't take a second deposit until the first applicant has withdrawn in writing.

title: Electric Submetering
bodyText: South Carolina has no submetering disclosure or billing rule for landlords. Two rules point the other way. First, electricity to new multi-unit residential buildings whose units are separately rented must be delivered by the utility through an individual meter for each dwelling, unless the Public Service Commission approves an exception because individual metering is impractical (buildings permitted or started before January 23, 1981, are grandfathered). Second, the utility law exempts someone who furnishes electricity to their own tenants only when the current is "not resold"; whether billing tenants by submeter is a resale that makes you a regulated electrical utility isn't settled by the statute. Cautious course: have the utility meter each unit; if an older building is master-metered, include electricity in the rent rather than reselling it by submeter, or get advice first. Utility accounts generally: `edu-utilities-sc`.

title: Screening Your Employees
bodyText: No South Carolina statute requires a landlord to run background checks on apartment staff, maintenance workers or leasing agents, or limits whom you may hire for those jobs. The only background-check rule in the area is for licensees: a property manager or property manager-in-charge licensed by the Real Estate Commission must submit to a criminal background check to be licensed and at every third renewal. Unlicensed employees of an owner may do only limited on-site tasks (`edu-no-landlord-registration-rule-sc`). Cautious course: screen anyone who will hold keys or enter units, and keep key-control records, since an employee's misconduct inside a tenant's home can lead to a negligent-hiring claim.

title: Who May Represent a Company Landlord in Court
bodyText: In magistrates court, where most South Carolina ejectment cases are heard, a corporation, partnership, LLC or other listed business entity (and a housing authority) may designate an employee or principal to represent it. The designation must be in writing and handed to the magistrate when the entity files its first pleading in the case; the designee is then not practicing law without a license. This was rewritten by 2026 Act No. 233, effective May 19, 2026. The statute doesn't cover an outside property management company acting for an owner (but separately, a licensed broker-in-charge or licensed property manager, or their regular employees, may complete a form writ of eviction and present facts to the magistrate for the owner in an eviction, distress or abandonment matter, if no separate charge is made; that isn't general representation at a contested hearing), and it doesn't reach circuit court (appeals and larger claims), where an entity should appear through a lawyer. An individual owner may always represent himself or herself.

title: Ending a Lease After an Environmental Event
bodyText: South Carolina has no statute letting a landlord end a lease after an environmental or public-health event (a chemical spill, contamination, a sewer failure) or a government order closing the building. The casualty statute gives only the tenant options: if a fire or casualty substantially impairs normal use, the tenant may move out and end the lease with written notice within seven days, or stay and pay reduced rent for the usable part (`edu-casualty-termination-sc`). You get a termination right only if the lease gives you one; the library's opt-in `casualty-landlord-termination-sc` clause does that for fire or casualty you didn't cause. A city order to vacate and close an unfit dwelling binds you as owner, but doesn't itself end the lease; if occupancy becomes unlawful, account for rent as of the order and return the deposit under the usual rules.

title: Conditions on Tenant EV Chargers
bodyText:
South Carolina gives tenants no right to install an electric-vehicle charger (`edu-no-ev-charging-right-sc`) and sets no rules on the conditions you may impose, so whether to allow one, and on what terms, is up to you and the lease.

Because a charger is an alteration, the lease's no-alterations term applies until you approve it in writing. Sensible conditions, which the library's `ev-charger-installation-conditions-nd` clause (carrying SC) sets out: a licensed electrician, permits and code compliance, your specifications for location and cabling, insurance naming you, the tenant paying for the electricity and any damage, and your right to refuse for capacity or safety reasons.

If you sell charging electricity to tenants yourself, you're not a regulated electrical utility as long as you buy the power from an authorized utility, furnish it only for charging plug-in vehicles, and the station is fixed in place.

title: EV Chargers in Shared Parking
bodyText: No South Carolina statute deals with a tenant's EV charger in a parking area other tenants use: no right to a space, no rule on reserving it, and no cost-sharing or liability rule. If you allow one, the lease sets the terms; the library's `ev-charging-shared-area-co` clause, which carries SC, lets you charge a reasonable fee to reserve the space where the charger goes and makes the tenant responsible for damage from the installation and its upkeep. Keep shared parking reasonably safe and, in buildings of more than four units, reasonably clean, which includes routing cables so they don't create a trip hazard. Condominium and HOA parking may need association approval (`edu-hoa-sc`).

title: EV Chargers When the Tenant Leaves
bodyText: No South Carolina statute says who owns a tenant-installed EV charger at the end of the lease or whether the tenant must remove it. Put it in the lease or the approval: who removes it, by when, that a licensed electrician leaves the wiring safe, and that the tenant restores the surfaces, reasonable wear and tear excepted. Restoration costs the tenant fails to pay are damages from the tenant's breach of the lease, which you may deduct from the deposit with the itemized 30-day notice (`edu-security-deposit-rules-sc`). If the tenant leaves a charger behind, a charger bolted and wired in as agreed may be treated as part of the property if the lease says so; a plug-in unit is personal property governed by the abandoned-property rules (`abandoned-property-sc`). Because whether equipment is a fixture is case law, the cautious course is a written removal-or-surrender choice signed when you approve the install.

title: A Tenant Running a Home Child Care
bodyText: South Carolina has no statute protecting a tenant's right to run a family child care home in a rental, or limiting what a landlord or association may require. The child care licensing law (administered by the state's social services agency) regulates the provider, not you: among other things, a family child care home without liability insurance must get each parent's signed acknowledgment that it carries none, and keep those statements at the home. Your lease controls: the residential-use term means a tenant needs your written consent to run a business, including child care (`residential-use-only`, `edu-home-business-sc`). If you consent, put the terms in writing (registration or licence, number of children, insurance naming you, use of yard and common areas), and check any HOA covenant (`edu-hoa-sc`). Refusing because the tenant has children is a different matter and is barred (`edu-children-occupancy-sc`).

title: Running a Business From a Rental
bodyText: South Carolina has no statute making a home-based business a permitted use of a rental or stopping a lease from restricting one. The Act's default is that, unless otherwise agreed, a tenant must occupy the unit only as a dwelling, and the library's `residential-use-only` clause (which carries SC) bars commercial use. So a tenant needs your agreement to run a business there; if you allow one, write down the business, customer traffic, signs, deliveries, licences, and any added insurance. Whether quiet work-from-home is "commercial use" isn't settled by statute; treat ordinary remote work as residential. Local zoning and business-licence rules for home occupations are local, and HOA covenants may add limits (`edu-hoa-sc`). Child care at home: `edu-family-child-care-sc`.

title: Which Fire Code Applies
bodyText: South Carolina has one statewide fire code. The Building Codes Council adopts the latest International Fire Code (with the building, residential and other International codes), and the State Fire Marshal's regulations make the IFC the minimum standard for fire prevention and life safety in the construction, occupancy and use of all buildings, private ones included; those minimums can't be waived. Cities and counties enforce these codes; a few older-building codes (property maintenance, existing building) are local options. As landlord you must comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, and a tenant must meet the code duties that fall on tenants. Smoke detectors are covered separately (`smoke-detectors-sc`): apartments without a fire protection system need detectors under one statute, and rented one- and two-family homes under another. Grills and open flames: `fire-safety-grilling`.

title: No Sprinkler Retrofit Duty
bodyText: South Carolina has no rule requiring a landlord to add fire sprinklers to an existing rental. Sprinklers are a construction-code matter: the state's residential code does not require automatic sprinklers in one- and two-family homes or townhouses, nor when existing ones are added to or altered, and by statute any such requirement for one- and two-family homes would have to be adopted as a regulation; larger apartment buildings follow the building and fire codes in force when built. What you must do in an existing building is keep any system that is installed in working order under the fire code, and, in an apartment house with no fire protection system, provide smoke detectors in each unit (`smoke-detectors-sc`). Owners who voluntarily install a sprinkler system may qualify for a 25% property-tax credit if the local taxing entity consents.

title: Firearms in a South Carolina Rental
bodyText:
No South Carolina statute stops a landlord from regulating firearms in a private rental, or protects a tenant's right to keep one there. The carry law preserves the right of a private property owner or person in legal possession or control to allow or prohibit carrying a concealable weapon on the premises, and posting a "NO CONCEALABLE WEAPONS ALLOWED" sign gives notice; knowingly carrying one in violation can be charged as trespass.

In a rental, the tenant is in legal possession of the unit and you control the common areas, so a common-area sign reaches visitors, while rules inside the unit need to be in the lease. The library's `firearm-rules-ks` clause, which carries SC, takes the middle course: no discharge except lawful defense, safe storage away from children, and liability for damage. A broader ban is lawful but harder to enforce.

title: When a Rental Is Foreclosed
bodyText:
South Carolina has no statute protecting a residential tenant when the landlord's mortgage is foreclosed, and no state notice to tenants of the foreclosure. Foreclosure here is a court case; a tenant in possession may be named and served, and after the sale the buyer takes subject to whatever rights the foreclosure decree leaves.

Federal law fills much of the gap: under the Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act, the buyer at foreclosure of a residential property generally takes subject to a bona fide lease and must give at least 90 days' notice to vacate (a tenant with a lease can stay to its end unless the buyer will live there).

If you sell rather than lose the property, the buyer becomes the landlord by statute (`edu-sale-of-rented-property-sc`). In a condominium, an association foreclosing its assessment lien may have a receiver collect rents (`edu-hoa-sc`). Tell tenants promptly if foreclosure is filed (`edu-no-adverse-proceeding-notice-sc`).

title: Foreign Owners and Tenants
bodyText: South Carolina doesn't require a lease to state whether a tenant is a nonresident alien, and has no recent foreign-adversary restriction on buying or leasing land. The old rule still on the books: an alien may acquire, hold and dispose of property like a citizen, but no alien or alien-controlled corporation may own or control more than 500,000 acres of land in the state (excess land acquired by foreclosing a mortgage must be sold within five years, extendable once). Ordinary residential leasing is untouched. If you are a nonresident owner, the state's rent withholding rules may apply (`edu-nonresident-landlord-withholding-sc`); asking about a tenant's immigration status isn't regulated by state law (`edu-no-immigration-inquiry-rule-sc`).

title: Which Edition of the Codes Applies
bodyText: South Carolina adopts its building codes by statewide edition, not as they change automatically. The Building Codes Council must adopt the latest editions of the International building, residential, gas, plumbing, mechanical, fire and energy codes and the National Electrical Code, but only after a published notice, a comment period of at least 180 days, a study committee and a council decision; the adopted code (with South Carolina modifications) is codified and takes effect on a January 1 or July 1 the Council sets. The regulations in force when this was written adopt the 2021 editions of the International Building, Residential and Fire Codes with state amendments. Other agencies that enforce a national code must also adopt its latest edition by State Register notice. For an existing rental, the code in force when it was built or altered generally governs; your continuing duty is to comply with codes materially affecting health and safety (`edu-fire-code-standard-sc`).

title: Tenants' Guests
bodyText:
South Carolina has no statute giving tenants a right to receive guests or service providers, limiting guest rules, or barring guest fees. The Act speaks of "persons on the premises with the tenant's permission": the tenant must make them behave so as not to disturb other tenants' peaceful enjoyment, and is responsible if the tenant knowingly lets them damage the premises.

Guest limits are therefore a lease matter (`guest-policy`, `guest-policy-day-limit`) and must meet the rule standards (`edu-rules-and-regulations-sc`): fair to all tenants, reasonably related to a proper purpose, and explicit. You may bar a specific non-tenant from common areas under the trespass law, but not keep the tenant's invited guests out of the unit (`edu-trespass-notice-sc`). Guest limits applied differently by race, family status, disability or another protected class would violate fair-housing law.

title: Contamination and Environmental Restrictions
bodyText: South Carolina doesn't require you to tell a tenant in an ordinary lease about soil or groundwater contamination, a Superfund or brownfield site, or a recorded environmental restriction on the property. Two related rules: (1) before a lease with an option to purchase a one-to-four-unit home is signed, the owner must give the state property-condition disclosure statement, which asks about known hazardous or toxic material, underground storage tanks and other environmental contamination; and (2) when a brownfield is cleaned up under a voluntary cleanup contract that leaves some contamination, the state may require a recorded restrictive covenant limiting the property's use, which stays in effect until the site is fully remediated for unrestricted use and binds whoever occupies the land. If your property carries such a covenant, the lease should make the tenant follow it, and you should disclose any contamination you know of that affects health or use, since your duty to keep the unit fit and habitable still applies.

title: Heat in a South Carolina Rental
bodyText: You must make reasonable heat available, along with running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times, unless the building isn't required by law to be equipped for heat or the heat is generated by an installation within the tenant's exclusive control and supplied by a direct utility connection (a unit with its own furnace on the tenant's gas or electric account). You must also keep heating facilities you supply in reasonably good and safe working order. Heat is an essential service: if you negligently or wilfully fail to provide it, the tenant may give written notice and buy reasonable amounts of heat (such as space heaters) and deduct the actual cost from rent, or recover reduced-value damages and attorney's fees. South Carolina sets no minimum indoor temperature or heating season. If the tenant controls the heat, the lease can require them to keep it on in cold weather (`cold-weather-vacate-notice-wy`).

title: No Waiver of Exemptions in a Lease
bodyText: South Carolina has no statute letting a tenant waive, in a lease, the debtor's exemptions that protect property from attachment, levy and sale (the homestead interest in a residence, a vehicle, household furnishings and other listed items, up to statutory dollar limits). The Constitution directs the General Assembly to provide those exemptions, and the statute grants them against any mesne or final court process. A lease clause waiving them has no statutory support and would likely be unenforceable; leave it out. Your remedies for unpaid rent are a money judgment collected subject to the exemptions, and ejectment (`edu-eviction-process-sc`); a landlord's lien or distress on the tenant's household goods is restricted (`edu-landlord-lien-sc`).

title: No Early Termination for Age or Illness
bodyText: South Carolina gives a tenant no statutory right to end a lease early because of age, illness, disability, or a move to a nursing home, assisted living or senior housing. The early-termination rights that do exist: a tenant (or co-tenant's victim) protected under the domestic-violence provisions (`edu-dv-lease-termination-sc`), servicemembers under federal and state law (`edu-servicemember-rights-sc`), and a tenant's casualty rights (`edu-casualty-termination-sc`). Otherwise a tenant who leaves early owes rent subject to your duty to make reasonable efforts to re-rent (`edu-abandonment-and-mitigation-sc`). A lease may offer an infirmity or care-facility release, and a disabled tenant may ask for one as a reasonable accommodation, which you must consider under fair-housing law (`edu-disability-accommodation-sc`).

title: Key Control
bodyText:
South Carolina has no key-control statute: no written key policy, master-key log or employee background-check requirement for apartment complexes (`edu-no-employee-screening-rule-sc`).

The lock rules that exist: a tenant may not change the locks without your permission, and you may enter only on the grounds the Act lists (`landlords-access`), so master keys must be used only for those entries. The library's `keys` clause (receipt, return, re-keying charge) and `lock-change-ak` clause (no lock change without your written agreement, with an emergency exception and keys within five days), both carrying SC, cover the lease side.

Cautious course: keep master keys secured and logged, re-key between tenants, and limit access to staff who need it, since a key misused by an employee can lead to a negligence claim.

title: State Lead Notices and Orders
bodyText:
On top of the federal pre-1978 lead disclosure (`lead-based-paint`), South Carolina's Childhood Lead Poisoning Prevention and Control Act works through the Department of Public Health (which took over the article from the former DHEC; the renaming took effect May 15, 2026).

When a child under six lives in a dwelling where a lead-based hazard has been identified, the department posts a notice of the hazard in a conspicuous place, which must stay up until the department finds the hazard remediated, gives written notice to the occupant, and orders you as owner to remediate within a reasonable time; you may appeal as a contested case.

While a unit is posted and under order, you may not rent or offer it for occupancy by children until the hazard is remediated, and you may not evict a family with children because the hazard became known during their tenancy. Knowing violations are misdemeanors (each day a separate offense), with civil penalties up to $1,000 a day. See `edu-lead-hazards-sc`.

title: No Lead-Safe Certification for Rentals
bodyText: South Carolina has no lead-safe certification, periodic lead inspection or lead-free registry for rentals; no state program requires you to have a unit inspected or certified before renting it. The state lead law acts only after a hazard is identified where a young child lives: the Department of Public Health posts the unit, notifies the occupant and orders you to remediate, and you may not rent a posted unit to a household with children until it's fixed (`edu-lead-state-notices-sc`). Federal rules still apply to pre-1978 housing: the lead disclosure and pamphlet at signing (`lead-based-paint`), and federal renovation, repair and painting work practices for contractors. Public water systems, not landlords, must tell customers about lead service lines.

title: What a South Carolina Lease Must Contain
bodyText: South Carolina sets no general list of required lease contents and no rule that the start and end dates appear on the first page. The few content rules: the owner-or-agent disclosure for notices and service of process; the posted or delivered deposit-standards statement if you use different standards for more than four adjoining units; the conspicuous periodic-services entry term if you want one; specific exclusion of any appliance you won't maintain; and the statutory "IF YOU DO NOT PAY YOUR RENT ON TIME" paragraph if you want the lease to be the nonpayment notice (`edu-required-disclosures-sc`). One first-page rule applies to some landlords: a real estate licensee renting out property in a personal transaction must reveal licence status in bold, underlined, capital letters on the first page of the lease. A lease of more than a year must be in a signed writing to be more than a tenancy at will (`edu-lease-term-limits-sc`).

title: Giving the Tenant a Copy of the Lease
bodyText:
South Carolina doesn't require a landlord to give the tenant a copy of the signed lease, and not doing so isn't a defense to enforcing it. (Self-storage operators must give a copy; a broker-in-charge or property manager-in-charge must keep a copy of each lease for at least five years and produce it to the Real Estate Commission on request.)

Giving a copy is still the cautious course: your rules bind the tenant only if the tenant had notice of them at signing or when adopted, and the statutory nonpayment paragraph works as notice only if it is in the written lease the tenant has. The library's `lease-copy-receipt-hi` clause, which carries SC, records that the tenant received the lease and rules and commits you to deliver a fully signed copy.

title: No Initials Requirement
bodyText: No South Carolina statute requires a tenant to initial any lease provision to make it enforceable. Where the law cares how a term looks, it asks for conspicuousness, not initials: the nonpayment-notice paragraph must be in conspicuous language (bold conspicuous type in the ejectment chapter) to replace the separate notice (`nonpayment-notice-sc`); the periodic-services entry right must be conspicuously in writing (`periodic-services-entry-sc`); and an arbitration clause needs notice in underlined capital letters on the first page (`edu-binding-arbitration-sc`). Having the tenant initial the notice-period, nonpayment and any unusual terms is still good evidence that they saw them.

title: Recording a Long Lease
bodyText: South Carolina has no lease registry, and recording doesn't change any right under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. The recording statute matters for long leases: a written lease between landlord and tenant for longer than twelve months is valid against later creditors and buyers for value without notice only from the day and hour it is recorded with the register of deeds (or clerk of court) in the county where the property is. So a tenant with a long lease who wants protection against a sale or mortgage the tenant doesn't know about may record it (or a memorandum, if the register accepts one). Leases of a year or less don't fall under that recording rule; a buyer of rented property generally becomes the landlord (`edu-sale-of-rented-property-sc`). Whether a tenant's possession alone gives a buyer notice is case law.

title: Long Leases: Writing and Term Limits
bodyText: South Carolina has no maximum term for a private residential lease, no spousal-consent or seal requirement, and no special formality for leases over a year beyond a signed writing. The writing rule is old but firm: a lease or term of years created only by word of mouth, not put in writing and signed by the parties (or their agents authorized in writing), has the force of an estate at will only, except leases of no more than one year from entry; and the statute of frauds bars suing on an unwritten contract for an interest in land or one that can't be performed within a year. So put every lease over a year in writing signed by the landlord and every tenant. A written lease longer than twelve months should also be recorded to bind later buyers and lenders (`edu-lease-recording-sc`). The only term cap is in the old Catawba lands statute (99 years or three lives, `edu-communal-land-lease-sc`).

title: Month-to-Month Versus Fixed-Term Terms
bodyText: No South Carolina statute requires month-to-month and fixed-term tenants to get the same terms, bars a month-to-month premium, or caps the rent difference between lease types.
