You may charge more for month-to-month, and rent amounts can't be regulated by cities or counties (`edu-local-preemption-sc`). The Act treats an agreement without a definite term as month to month (week to week for a roomer paying weekly), ended by 30 (or 7) days' written notice (`edu-periodic-tenancy-notice-sc`), and a lease's statutory nonpayment paragraph carries over into a month-to-month tenancy after the term. Offering different terms by race, family status, disability or another protected class is barred.

title: No Minimum Type Size for Leases
bodyText: South Carolina sets no minimum type size for a residential lease and no penalty for small print. The rules on how lease terms look are specific: the nonpayment-notice paragraph must be conspicuous to replace the separate notice; the periodic-services entry right must be conspicuously in writing; a licensee renting out their own property must state licence status in bold, underlined capitals on the first page; and an arbitration clause needs a first-page notice in underlined capitals. A clause buried in tiny print is also more open to an unconscionability challenge (`edu-unconscionability-sc`). Use a readable font throughout.

title: No Inspection-Notice Penalty
bodyText: South Carolina doesn't require you to tell a tenant about a right to a move-in or move-out inspection, so there is no penalty for leaving such a notice out, and no rule makes you forfeit the right to deduct from the deposit for skipping an inspection (`edu-no-move-in-inspection-rule-sc`). The penalty that does exist is in the deposit statute: if you don't return the deposit with the itemized written notice within 30 days, the tenant may recover three times the amount wrongfully withheld plus reasonable attorney's fees (`edu-security-deposit-penalty-sc`). Inspections are still your best evidence for deductions: do a dated, signed walk-through with photos at move-in and move-out.

title: Working With Law Enforcement
bodyText: No South Carolina statute requires a landlord to join a crime-free housing program, give police access to units or records, or evict on police request, and none bars a lease from penalizing a tenant who calls the police (`edu-no-police-call-protection-sc`). What state law gives you: illegal activity by a tenant is a five-day termination ground (`edu-no-expedited-criminal-eviction-sc`); a building used for repeated drug or other listed offenses can be closed as a nuisance after notice to the owner (`edu-nuisance-sc`); you may enter with a law enforcement officer only to serve ejectment papers, by court order or on the other grounds the Act lists; and officers enforce the trespass law for people you've warned off common areas (`edu-trespass-notice-sc`). Police need a warrant or the tenant's consent to enter a tenant's home; don't consent for the tenant. Local crime-free ordinances are local.

title: Time Limits for Suing
bodyText: In South Carolina most landlord-tenant money claims must be brought within three years: that is the period for an action on a contract, obligation or liability (unpaid rent, damages for breach of the lease, a tenant's deposit claim), for a liability created by statute other than a penalty, and for damage to real property. A lease signed under seal can carry a 20-year period, but not a sealed promise to pay money only. A later written acknowledgment or promise signed by the tenant, or any part payment, restarts the clock. Time a debtor spends out of the state after the claim accrues (absent for a year or more) doesn't count. The clock generally runs from when the claim accrues (each rent installment when due). Ejectment itself has no limitation problem while the tenant remains in possession.

title: Military Bases and Noise Zones
bodyText: South Carolina has no lease (or sale) disclosure for property near a military air installation or in a noise or accident-potential zone, and no tenant right to end a lease over one. The state's tools near bases are planning ones: local governments may buy or accept residential development rights near an operating military base to prevent encroachment, and local zoning may restrict development. Near an air base, the cautious course is to tell prospective tenants about aircraft noise you know of, since the general unfair trade practices law reaches deception in leasing real property (`edu-consumer-protection-act-sc`). Local planning rules are local.

title: Liens for a Tenant's Unpaid Sewer Bills
bodyText: Under South Carolina law a tenant is solely responsible for gas, electric, water, sewer and garbage service to the leased premises unless you agree otherwise in writing, a provider may not make you sign up to guarantee the tenant's account or cut service because you refuse, and you aren't liable on the tenant's account; none of these rules applies to a building of four or more residential units served by a master meter or single connection. But sewer service charges are different where a city council, special purpose district or county sewer authority has followed the statutory notice-and-hearing procedure: unpaid sewer charges then become a lien on the real estate served, superior to all liens except property taxes, enforceable like a tax lien. No statute exempts the owner's property from that lien when the tenant ran up the bill, and there is no affidavit procedure to avoid it. Cautious course: ask the sewer provider whether its charges are lien charges, require proof the tenant's account is current (`utility-payment-evidence`), and check before the tenant moves out.

title: Conduct While a Notice to Vacate Runs
bodyText: South Carolina has no statute limiting what a landlord may do while a notice to vacate is pending: no bar on alterations that make the unit uninhabitable, no rule on showing it more often, and no added notice content. The ordinary rules continue until the tenancy ends: you must keep the unit fit and habitable and supply essential services, wilfully cutting services to force a tenant out is an unlawful ouster (`edu-no-rent-lockout-sc`), entry still needs 24 hours' notice except in the listed cases, and a notice served in retaliation for protected complaints is barred (`edu-retaliation-sc`). If code compliance requires work that would deprive the tenant of the unit, the retaliation statute recognizes that you may end the tenancy for it.

title: Defaults Your Lease Can Change
bodyText: Several South Carolina rules apply only "unless otherwise agreed" or only if the lease opts in, so they are real choices: (1) rent is payable at the unit, at the start of each period of a month or less and otherwise in equal monthly installments, and apportioned day to day, unless the lease or a written notice says otherwise; (2) without a definite term the tenancy is month to month (week to week for a weekly roomer); (3) the tenant must use the unit only as a dwelling unless otherwise agreed; (4) entry for scheduled periodic services without consent, only if conspicuous in the lease (`periodic-services-entry-sc`); (5) the statutory nonpayment paragraph in place of a separate notice (`nonpayment-notice-sc`); (6) for a single-family home, a written agreement shifting appliance and facility upkeep and specified repairs to the tenant (`tenant-repair-agreement-sc`); (7) a landlord termination right after fire or casualty (`casualty-landlord-termination-sc`); and (8) bona fide liquidated damages for early termination (`edu-liquidated-damages-sc`). A lease with an option to purchase a one-to-four-unit home triggers the property-condition disclosure (`edu-no-contamination-disclosure-sc`). What a lease can't change: `edu-prohibited-lease-terms-sc`.

title: Ordnance, Demolition and Shared-Meter Disclosures
bodyText: South Carolina requires none of three disclosures some places require: no notice that the property is near a former military ordnance site, no notice to prospective tenants that you have applied to demolish the building, and no notice that the tenant's gas or electric meter also serves other areas. Related rules: if you rely on a meter conservation charge on the utility account, you must give the tenant written notice (`meter-conservation-charge-notice-sc`); shared-area lighting on the tenant's service is a lease term (`common-area-lighting-ks`); and if housing-code compliance requires demolition that would deprive the tenant of the unit, you may end the tenancy for that reason without it being retaliation (`edu-retaliation-sc`). Disclose known conditions anyway; concealment risks an unfair-practice claim.

title: Laundry Rooms, Pools, Elevators and Other Facilities
bodyText: South Carolina has no amenity statute. The Act's general duties reach any facility you supply: you must keep electrical, gas, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, supplied or required to be supplied by you in reasonably good and safe working order, and keep common areas reasonably safe (and, with more than four units, reasonably clean). Facilities held out for tenants generally are part of the "premises". No statute governs garage door openers, closing a pool for the season, or charging for amenities in an apartment lease (a park owner can't add a fee for an amenity that was included in lot rent). List the facilities in the lease, say when they may close for repair, safety or season, and apply amenity rules fairly to all tenants (`edu-rules-and-regulations-sc`); a rule limiting children's use of facilities must be justified by safety, not familial status. Elevators are inspected by the state.

title: Other Rules South Carolina Does Not Have
bodyText: Rules found elsewhere that South Carolina doesn't have, each explained in its own row with what the state does have nearby: no agreed actual-notice method (`edu-no-agreed-notice-method-rule-sc`); no duty to tell tenants of proceedings against the property (`edu-no-adverse-proceeding-notice-sc`); no alternative-housing duty (`edu-no-alt-housing-duty-sc`); no auto-renewal rule (`edu-no-automatic-renewal-rule-sc`); no double-letting rule (`edu-no-double-letting-rule-sc`); no cold-weather or extended-absence notice (`edu-no-cold-weather-vacate-notice-sc`); no infirmity termination (`edu-no-infirmity-termination-sc`); no lease-copy, initials or type-size rules (`edu-no-lease-copy-duty-sc`, `edu-no-lease-initials-requirement-sc`, `edu-no-lease-type-size-sc`); no lease-type parity (`edu-no-lease-type-parity-sc`); no limits while a notice to vacate runs (`edu-no-notice-to-vacate-terms-rule-sc`); no guest-rights statute (`edu-no-guest-rights-statute-sc`); no key-control or employee-screening mandate (`edu-no-key-control-policy-sc`, `edu-no-employee-screening-rule-sc`); and no waiver of debtor exemptions (`edu-no-homestead-waiver-sc`). Where the law is silent, the lease governs within the Act's limits.

title: Notice of Pest Control Treatment
bodyText: No South Carolina statute requires you to give tenants a pesticide notice with the lease, to pass on an exterminator's notice, or to tell tenants which product will be used. The Act's entry rules apply instead: you may enter without the tenant's consent between 9 a.m. and 6 p.m. for regularly scheduled pest treatment only if the lease sets out that right conspicuously in writing and you announce your intent before entering (`periodic-services-entry-sc`); for any other treatment visit give at least 24 hours' notice and enter at reasonable times. The state Pesticide Control Act licenses applicators and lets the regulator require notice of restricted-use pesticide applications to adjoining landowners. The applicator rules (Code of Regulations chapter 27, Clemson University's pesticide rules) set no tenant notice; they require anyone doing structural pest control in rented or leased housing, such as apartment complexes, to be licensed or supervised by a licensee. Cautious course: tell tenants the date, the product and any re-entry time on its label before each treatment.

title: No Pets-and-Eviction Fact Sheet
bodyText: No South Carolina statute requires you to give a tenant with a dog or cat a fact sheet about caring for pets in an eviction, and no statute deals with pets during an ejectment. The eviction-property rule covers only belongings put on the street (`edu-post-eviction-property-sc`), and the abandoned-property rule doesn't mention animals (`abandoned-property-sc`). The general animal law still applies to the owner: abandoning an animal without securing another owner or providing food, water and shelter is a misdemeanor. Cautious course: tell the tenant before the writ is executed that any animal must leave with them, and if one is left behind, don't release it or dispose of it yourself; call local animal control.

title: No Plain-Language Lease Law
bodyText: South Carolina has no plain-language or readability law for residential leases: no rule that the lease use everyday words, be divided into captioned sections, meet a type size, or carry a front-page list of landlord-protective terms. The state Consumer Protection Code's disclosure rules reach consumer credit and leases of goods, not leases of homes. What does apply: a clause the court finds unconscionable when made may be refused enforcement (`edu-unconscionability-sc`), terms barred by the Act are unenforceable whatever their wording (`edu-prohibited-lease-terms-sc`), rules bind a tenant only if explicit enough to tell them what to do, and the general unfair-trade-practices law bars deceptive practices. Cautious course: write the lease in clear, short sentences and put key money terms where the tenant will see them.

title: No Statement of Consumer Restrictions
bodyText: South Carolina doesn't require a residential lease to carry a statement of consumer restrictions (a list of what the tenant could lose by defaulting), to pass a readability test, or to be preapproved by the Attorney General. There is no plain-language statute for leases at all (`edu-no-plain-language-rule-sc`). The state limits what a lease may contain rather than how it is phrased: a lease can't make the tenant waive rights under the Act, confess judgment, or excuse or indemnify you for your own legal liability, and a landlord who knowingly uses such terms and tries to enforce them can owe the tenant extra damages and attorney's fees (`edu-prohibited-lease-terms-sc`).

title: Candidates and Canvassers at Your Property
bodyText: No South Carolina statute requires you to let political candidates, campaign workers, petition circulators or voter-registration workers into an apartment building or gated community to reach tenants' doors, or to set aside space for campaign literature. Access by outsiders to common areas is your decision as the person in possession (`edu-trespass-notice-sc`), but a tenant may invite anyone into their own unit. If you adopt a no-soliciting or access rule, it must meet the Act's test for enforceable rules: reasonably related to tenants' convenience, safety or welfare, explicit, and applied to all tenants fairly, so apply it the same way to every campaign and cause.

title: Pools at Rental Properties
bodyText: South Carolina regulates pools by type, not through the lease. A pool at an apartment complex, condominium development or mobile home park is a public swimming pool under the State Recreational Waters Act: it needs a construction permit and an annual operating permit from the Department of Environmental Services, and the owner must keep the water safe and the pool free of hazards and keep operating records. The Department's pool regulation (61-51) classes these as Type B pools, requires at least a four-foot fence with gates that close and latch automatically and can be locked, "NO LIFEGUARD ON DUTY - SWIM AT YOUR OWN RISK" signs where there is no lifeguard, posted pool rules and a credentialed pool operator. A pool built with a single-family rental house is a residential pool, outside these rules. No statute requires a pool safety notice in the lease. Pool rules bind tenants under the Act's rules test (`edu-rules-and-regulations-sc`), and a lease can't excuse you from liability for an unsafe common area.

title: Window and Portable Air Conditioners
bodyText: South Carolina gives tenants no right to install a window or portable air conditioner, and no statute limits a lease rule restricting them or sets a heat-event rule. Air conditioning isn't one of the Act's essential services (heat and hot water are), but if you supply it, you must keep it in good and safe working order, and an appliance in the unit is presumed supplied by you unless the lease specifically excludes it (`appliances-excluded-sc`). So you may allow tenant-owned units on conditions (secure mounting, no blocked exit window, tenant pays for damage) or bar window units in the lease or rules, applied to all tenants fairly. A tenant who needs cooling because of a disability may ask for a reasonable accommodation or modification under the Fair Housing Law (`edu-fair-housing-sc`).

title: Plug-In and Balcony Solar Devices
bodyText: South Carolina gives tenants no right to install a plug-in, balcony or portable solar device, and no statute voids a lease or covenant restriction on solar equipment. The state's solar statutes deal with utility net-metering programs and with solar companies that lease systems to customers, not with tenants. So the lease may bar solar and other generating equipment or allow it only with your written consent on conditions you set (safe attachment, no roof or wall penetration, removal and repair at move-out, tenant pays for damage). Under the Act, the tenant must not damage the premises and must use electrical facilities reasonably. A disability-related request for a modification is handled under the Fair Housing Law (`edu-fair-housing-sc`).

title: Private Wells at Rental Properties
bodyText: No South Carolina statute or regulation requires you to test a private well serving a rental, or to give a tenant well test results or well-water information. The Department of Environmental Services' well standards (regulation 61-71) govern how individual residential wells are built, disinfected and maintained, not what you tell tenants; the well-permitting regulation (61-44) has the Department inspect new wells and give the owner a copy of its inspection results, with nothing on tenants. A well system serving more than one home can be a regulated water system under the State Safe Drinking Water Act, which excludes only a system serving a single private residence; check with the Department before relying on one well for several units. You must keep water running and safe as part of a fit and habitable home (`edu-landlord-repair-duties-sc`), and an abandoned well on the property must not be left open and unprotected. Cautious course: test a well before a new tenancy and give the tenant a copy of the result.

title: Promises to Repair or Clean Before Move-In
bodyText: South Carolina has no rule that a promise to clean, repair or improve the unit must be in writing, carry a completion date, or be made before the lease is signed. But the Act counts every agreement, written or oral, as part of the rental agreement, so a repair you promise is a term you must keep. If you don't, the tenant may give a 14-day written notice to remedy a material breach or end the lease, and may sue for actual damages and an injunction (with attorney's fees if the failure is wilful) (`edu-landlord-breach-remedy-sc`). The lease's entire-agreement clause (`entire-agreement`) will be argued against an oral promise, so the cautious course is to list each promised item and its completion date in the lease or a signed addendum.

title: No Chemical-Exposure Warning for Rentals
bodyText: South Carolina has no Proposition 65-style rule requiring a landlord to warn tenants about chemicals in the building, and no formaldehyde or building-materials health notice for new housing. The disclosures that do apply are the federal lead-based paint disclosure for older housing (`lead-based-paint`, `edu-lead-hazards-sc`) and the owner and agent disclosure (`landlord-disclosure-sc`). If you know of a hazard in the unit, the Act's fitness and repair duties still apply (`edu-landlord-repair-duties-sc`).

title: No Property-Tax Share of Rent Statement
bodyText: South Carolina has no renter's property-tax credit or rebate, so you have no duty to give tenants a yearly statement of the share of their rent that goes to property taxes, on request or otherwise. Property taxes on a rental are your cost as owner; whether you pass increases on is a matter of rent and the lease terms. Tenants may ask for such a statement for other reasons, but nothing requires you to provide one.

title: Questions About Protected Characteristics
bodyText: South Carolina has no separate ban on asking about or recording an applicant's protected characteristics. The Fair Housing Law instead bars any notice or statement about a rental that indicates a preference, limitation or discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, handicap, familial status or national origin, which can reach an application form or interview question. The law expressly lets the application ask the number, ages, sex and family relationship of the applicants and intended occupants, and whether any intended occupant has a conviction for illegally making or distributing a controlled substance. For an animal that isn't a service animal, you may ask whether the person has a disability and a disability-related need for it, and ask for documentation. Cautious course: ask only what your screening criteria use, and don't ask about disability, religion or national origin otherwise. See `edu-fair-housing-sc` and `edu-no-immigration-inquiry-rule-sc`.

title: Prohibited Uses of the Premises
bodyText: No South Carolina statute makes a residential lease void, or ends it automatically, when the premises are used for a prohibited purpose. The Act itself limits use: unless otherwise agreed, a tenant must occupy the unit only as a dwelling and must not conduct or permit illegal activity there, and a breach lets you end the lease on the five-day track, then file for ejectment (see `edu-cure-and-eviction-grounds-sc` on the cure question) (`edu-no-expedited-criminal-eviction-sc`). Criminal and nuisance law reaches you too: anyone who owns or leases a building used for lewdness, prostitution, repeated drug sales or continuous breach of the peace is guilty of a nuisance, and the court can order the building closed for a year (`edu-nuisance-sc`); knowingly leasing a place intended for prostitution is a crime. Act promptly when you learn of illegal use.

title: No Recycling Notice Duty
bodyText: No South Carolina statute requires you to provide recycling at a rental, to tell tenants where and how to recycle, or to make tenants separate recyclables or food waste. Recycling programs are run by local governments under the state solid-waste law, and any rule for apartment recycling is local, not covered here (`edu-local-preemption-sc`). The Act requires the tenant to dispose of garbage and other waste in a reasonably clean and safe manner, and for buildings with more than four units requires you to keep the common areas reasonably clean. If you supply recycling containers, a lease rule telling tenants how to use them is enforceable if it meets the Act's rules test (`edu-rules-and-regulations-sc`).

title: Religious and Cultural Displays
bodyText: South Carolina has no statute giving tenants a right to display religious or cultural items (such as a mezuzah on the doorframe) or limiting a lease rule on door decorations. The only display right in state law is for the United States flag: any tenant may display one portable, removable U.S. flag in a respectful manner, whatever the lease says (`edu-tenant-display-rights-sc`). The Fair Housing Law bars discrimination in the terms or conditions of a rental because of religion, so a decoration rule must be neutral and applied evenly; a rule that singles out religious items, or is enforced only against one faith, invites a claim. Cautious course: allow small items on the door or frame and limit only size, placement and damage.

title: Flags, Signs and Displays
bodyText: South Carolina gives tenants one display right: whatever the lease, your rules or an association's covenants say, a tenant may display one portable, removable United States flag in a respectful manner, consistent with the federal flag code, on the premises the tenant is entitled to use. The statute doesn't say a landlord may limit size or placement, so don't use a rule that would keep a tenant from displaying the flag at all; a rule that only stops damage to the building is safer. No statute gives tenants a right to other flags, banners, political or religious displays (`edu-no-religious-display-rule-sc`), so the lease may limit them by rules applied the same way to every tenant. Don't remove a tenant's campaign sign yourself before an election: removing a lawfully placed political campaign sign without the candidate's or party's permission is a misdemeanor. Ask the tenant to take it down.

title: Reporting Rent Payments to Credit Bureaus
bodyText: South Carolina has no rent-reporting law: no duty to offer tenants positive rent reporting, no state program a tenant can be made to join, and no state rule requiring notice before you report late rent to a credit bureau. The state's consumer identity theft protection chapter deals with security freezes and identity theft, not with what landlords report. If you report rent, the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act governs the accuracy of what you furnish and disputes. Cautious course: say in the lease whether you report rent payments and to whom, and report only amounts that are actually due under the lease.

title: Sales Tax on Rent
bodyText: South Carolina doesn't tax ordinary residential rent. Its sales tax reaches the rental of rooms, lodgings and sleeping accommodations furnished to transients, at 7%, by any hotel, residence or other place, and rent paid by the same person for a period of 90 continuous days is not from a transient. So a lease of a home or apartment to one tenant for 90 days or more is outside the tax; a shorter furnished or vacation rental is taxed, and you, as the person in the business of furnishing accommodations, owe the tax. Exceptions: a home of fewer than six sleeping rooms that is your own residence, and rentals so short that federal law excludes the income (the 14-day rule). Cities and counties may add a local accommodations tax of up to 3% on the same transient rentals by ordinance. Such short stays are also outside the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (`edu-scope-exclusions-sc`, `edu-seasonal-tenancy-sc`).

title: Rules for Requiring Renter's Insurance
bodyText:
South Carolina has no statute regulating a lease requirement that the tenant carry renter's insurance: no rule that the tenant may pick the insurer, no limit on buying force-placed coverage and charging it to the tenant, no deadline for proof, and no required notice that your insurance doesn't cover the tenant's belongings. You may require coverage in the lease (`tenants-property-insurance-ks-oh-ca`).

Two limits apply: a lease can't make the tenant excuse you from, or indemnify you for, your own legal liability, so insurance terms must not work as a release; and your insurer generally can't sue the tenant for damage it pays you for unless the tenant caused it intentionally or recklessly (`edu-tenant-insurance-claims-sc`).

Cautious course: let the tenant choose the insurer, and charge only the actual cost of any coverage you buy after the tenant fails to give proof.

title: Your Insurer's Claims Against the Tenant
bodyText: If a tenant damages the rental and your insurer pays you for the loss under your policy, South Carolina bars the insurer from suing the tenant to recover what it paid, unless the tenant caused the damage intentionally or in reckless disregard of the rights of others. The bar covers damage to the real property and to your personal property leased with it, and it applies notwithstanding any other law, so a lease clause making the tenant answer to your insurer for ordinary negligence won't revive the claim. It doesn't stop you from recovering from the tenant (or the deposit) a loss your insurance didn't pay, such as the deductible, and the tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage the premises. Tell tenants that your policy doesn't cover their belongings or their liability (`tenants-property-insurance-ks-oh-ca`).

title: How Tenants Give Repair Notices
bodyText: In South Carolina the tenant's repair remedies start with a written notice: the 14-day notice to remedy a material breach or end the lease, the notice of a failure of essential services, and a written notice of a deficient smoke detector, which you must repair or replace within 15 days. A notice reaches you when it is delivered at your place of business or any place you hold out for receiving it, so name that address (and any email or portal you accept) in the lease (`landlord-disclosure-sc`, `notices`). Your duty to keep the unit fit and habitable doesn't wait for a written request, and under the Act you have notice of a condition you actually know about or have reason to know exists, so don't rely on a written-request clause to excuse a repair you knew was needed. A lease can set a channel for routine requests, but can't make it the only way to give a statutory notice or waive the written-notice remedies (`edu-tenant-repair-remedies-sc`).

title: Ending a Lease Because Repairs Cost Too Much
bodyText: No South Carolina statute lets you (or the tenant) end a residential lease because repairs would cost more than a set amount or a share of the property's value, and none limits the tenant's repair remedies by cost. Your duty to keep the unit fit and habitable has no cost ceiling. The nearest rules: after a fire or casualty that substantially impairs use, the tenant may vacate and end the lease, and the lease may give you an opt-in right to end it too (`casualty-landlord-termination-sc`); and where complying with a building or housing code requires alteration, remodeling or demolition that would effectively deprive the tenant of the unit, you may bring an action for possession even after a tenant's code complaint. A month-to-month tenancy can be ended on the ordinary written notice (`edu-periodic-tenancy-notice-sc`).

title: No Small-Landlord Repair Remedy Exemption
bodyText: South Carolina has no rent-escrow remedy that a tenant can start to force repairs, and no exemption a small landlord can claim by giving a notice (as some states allow for owners of three or four units). The Act's repair remedies apply to every landlord it covers: the tenant's 14-day notice to remedy or end the lease, damages and injunction, and the essential-services remedies; it expressly doesn't allow repair-and-deduct. The only rent payment into a case is in your ejectment action: a tenant who raises defenses must keep paying rent as it comes due, with the court setting the amount if you disagree. See `edu-tenant-repair-remedies-sc` and `edu-rent-into-court-counterclaim-sc`.

title: No State Rights and Responsibilities Guide
bodyText: South Carolina doesn't publish a landlord-tenant rights and responsibilities guide that you must give tenants before signing or at renewal, and no statute requires a signed acknowledgment of one. What the state requires you to disclose in writing is set out in `edu-required-disclosures-sc` (chiefly the owner and agent for notices and service, `landlord-disclosure-sc`). The state doesn't bar cities or counties from requiring a local handout; any such rule is local and isn't covered here. If you give tenants an informational summary voluntarily, make sure it doesn't misstate the Act.

title: No Statement of Tenant Rights
bodyText: No South Carolina statute requires a state-agency statement of tenant rights (or a tenants' bill of rights) to be attached to the lease, signed by the tenant, or given before you can sue. The state's lease-content rules are few: the written owner and agent disclosure (`landlord-disclosure-sc`), the bold lease paragraph that can replace a separate nonpayment notice (`nonpayment-notice-sc`), and a conspicuous written clause if you want to enter for regularly scheduled services without notice (`periodic-services-entry-sc`); see `edu-required-disclosures-sc`. Cities and counties aren't barred from adopting their own disclosure rules, but none is covered here.

title: No Notice of Code Variances
bodyText: No South Carolina statute or held regulation requires you to tell tenants about, or attach to the lease, a variance or exception from a building, housing, fire or health code granted for the property. Building codes are adopted and enforced locally under state law, and local housing-code variance procedures (and any tenant notice they require) are left to local ordinance, not covered here. Your duty under the Act is to comply with applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, so a variance the code authority grants changes what compliance means; keep a copy and give it to a tenant who asks.

title: Seasonal and Vacation Rentals
bodyText: South Carolina has no special seasonal-tenancy rule (no nonrenewable seasonal lease form, no faster eviction), but short stays fall under a separate law. The Vacation Rental Act covers renting a house, condo, cottage or apartment for fewer than 90 days, other than a weekly or monthly rental under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. A vacation rental needs a written agreement, accepted by the tenant's signature, a payment or taking possession; a rental management company must hold the tenant's money in a trust account and may collect rent, deposit and fees in advance, which may be nonrefundable if the agreement says so. The tenant must obey a mandatory evacuation order, and a buyer takes the property subject to vacation rentals starting within 90 days after recording. Such stays carry the transient accommodations tax (`edu-rent-tax-sc`) and are outside the Act (`edu-scope-exclusions-sc`). A seasonal lease of 90 days or more is an ordinary fixed-term tenancy under the Act: it ends on its end date, and holding over triggers the Act's holdover rules (`edu-holdover-remedies-sc`).

title: Locks and Security Devices
bodyText: South Carolina has no security-device statute: no list of required locks, deadbolts, window latches or door viewers, and no duty to rekey between tenants. What applies: you must comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety and keep the unit fit and habitable, and locally adopted property-maintenance codes may require working locks (local matters aren't covered here); and the tenant may not change the locks without your permission. A domestic-violence victim has no statutory right to a lock change (`edu-no-dv-lockchange-rule-sc`). The lease's keys clause covers issuing and returning keys and charging to rekey when keys aren't returned (`keys`). Cautious course: rekey or change locks between tenants, fix a reported broken lock promptly, and give the tenant a key to any lock you approve.

title: Smart Locks and Electronic Entry
bodyText: No South Carolina statute regulates smart locks, keypads, fobs, app-based or biometric entry in rentals: none requires a non-app or non-biometric alternative, limits use of entry records, or lets a domestic-violence victim make you cut off another person's app access. The general rules apply. Entering through an electronic lock is still entry, so you need the tenant's consent, an emergency, or at least 24 hours' notice and a reasonable time (or the conspicuous periodic-services clause) (`landlords-access`); cutting off a tenant's access to force them out is an unlawful lockout (`edu-no-rent-lockout-sc`); and the tenant may not change or add locks without your permission. If you keep entry logs with personal identifying information, protect them (`edu-tenant-records-sc`). Cautious course: offer a physical key or code backup and say in the lease what the system records.

title: No Criminal Penalty for Refusing an Assistance Dog in Housing
bodyText: South Carolina makes it a misdemeanor to deny or interfere with a disabled person's admittance to the public places listed in the White Cane Law (including hotels and lodging places), but that penalty doesn't reach rental housing. For housing, the law gives a disabled person with an assistance dog full and equal access to all housing accommodations offered for rent, with no extra charge for the dog, while the person is liable for damage the dog causes. A refusal is enforced as housing discrimination under the Fair Housing Law (a refusal to make a reasonable accommodation), not as a crime. Short-term lodging may be a lodging place under the public-access rule, so treat a vacation rental as covered by the misdemeanor. Never refuse or charge a pet fee for an assistance dog; see `assistance-animal-accommodation-sc` and `edu-service-animal-law-sc`.

title: Misrepresenting an Animal as a Service Animal
bodyText: South Carolina makes it unlawful to knowingly and intentionally misrepresent an animal as a service animal (or one in training) to obtain a right or privilege provided to a disabled person. It is a civil violation, not a crime: fines of up to $250 for a first offense, $500 for a second and $1,000 after that, with no arrest except on a warrant for failing to appear or pay. The statute isn't limited by its words to public accommodations, so it can reach a false claim made to get housing, but enforcement inquiries are limited to the questions the federal public-accommodation rule allows. A misrepresentation fine is for the court; it doesn't let you refuse an animal the tenant is entitled to as a reasonable accommodation. For an emotional support animal you may ask the two disability questions and request documentation (`edu-service-animal-law-sc`, `assistance-animal-accommodation-sc`).

title: Staff in Housing for Older Persons
bodyText: No South Carolina statute requires a work card, license or background check for staff who work in 55-plus or 62-plus housing, or in any other ordinary rental housing. The state rules that matter for such housing are in the Fair Housing Law: its familial-status protections don't apply to housing for older persons, defined as housing in a qualifying government program for the elderly, housing intended for and solely occupied by people 62 or older, or housing intended and operated for occupancy by at least one person 55 or older per unit, under the Human Affairs Commission's regulations. Cautious course: screen staff who will hold keys under a written, consistently applied policy.

title: Sex Offender Registry Information
bodyText: South Carolina doesn't require a landlord to put a sex offender registry notice in the lease or to tell tenants that a registered offender lives nearby; the registry law says it imposes no duty on anyone outside the officials who run it to disclose registry information. A real estate brokerage (including one that leases for you) is immune from liability over registry disclosure if it gives its clients and customers timely written notice that they can get registry information from the county sheriff. Registry information is public, and an owner selling property isn't liable for failing to disclose it. Cautious course: include a one-line notice that registry information is available from the county sheriff, and never misstate what you know if a tenant asks.

title: Registered Offenders as Occupants
bodyText: South Carolina puts the residency limit on the offender, not on you. A sex offender convicted of criminal sexual conduct with a minor (first or second degree), assault with intent to commit it, or kidnapping or trafficking a person under 18 may not reside within 1,000 feet of a school, daycare center, children's recreational facility, park or public playground, measured in a straight line from the property to the facility's property line. Exceptions include offenders who lived there before the law took effect or before the facility opened. Police give the offender 30 days to move; staying is a crime for the offender. Cities and counties can't widen or narrow those zones. No statute makes it a crime for a landlord to rent to an offender or to let two offenders live together, but helping a person who isn't complying with registration elude law enforcement is a felony. Screening on criminal records is your choice under a consistent policy (`edu-tenant-screening-sc`).

title: Deaths, Illness and Other Stigmas
bodyText: South Carolina protects owners and real estate licensees from claims for not disclosing that a property is psychologically affected. No cause of action arises against an owner or licensed agent in a transaction for failing to disclose that an occupant had a disease medical evidence shows is highly unlikely to spread through occupancy (such as HIV), that an occupant died there or how, an off-site condition that doesn't directly affect the property, or a psychological impact with no material effect on its physical condition; a parallel rule in the seller-disclosure law covers sales and lease-purchases and adds public sex offender registry information. Neither rule protects an intentional misrepresentation in answer to a direct question. Cautious course for a lease: you needn't volunteer these facts, but answer a tenant's direct question truthfully or decline to answer; never misstate. Don't refer to a past occupant's HIV status; disability is protected by the Fair Housing Law (`edu-fair-housing-sc`).

title: Screening Applicants
bodyText: South Carolina has no tenant-screening statute: no rule that criminal-history checks wait for a conditional offer, no look-back periods, no limit on minimum-income tests, no application-fee cap (`edu-no-application-fee-cap-sc`), and no shield from negligence claims for renting to someone with a record. What applies: (1) the Fair Housing Law: use the same written criteria for every applicant and don't screen on race, color, religion, sex, familial status, national origin or handicap; you may refuse someone whose tenancy would pose a real and present threat of substantial harm or a direct threat, and may act on a conviction for illegally making or distributing a controlled substance (`edu-protected-class-inquiry-sc`); (2) an expunged arrest or charge restores the person to their prior legal status, so don't hold it against them; (3) eviction records are removed from the public index after seven years from January 1, 2027 (`edu-eviction-record-removal-sc`); and (4) the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act's adverse-action notice when a consumer report affects your decision. The state doesn't bar local screening rules; none is covered here.

title: No Single-Family Rental Occupancy Disclosure
bodyText: South Carolina has no special disclosure for renting a single-family house: no notice about lawful occupancy or squatting presumptions, and no rule setting a disclosure's type size relative to the rest of the lease or requiring it on the first page. Squatters are handled by the 2026 unlawful-occupant procedure, which needs no lease notice (`edu-unauthorized-occupant-removal-sc`). The one first-page rule in state law is for real estate licensees: a licensee renting property in a personal transaction must reveal their license status in bold, underlined capital letters on the first page of the lease. The Act's single-family definition matters elsewhere, for the written agreement shifting maintenance to the tenant (`tenant-repair-agreement-sc`).

title: Beachfront Property Disclosures
bodyText: No South Carolina statute requires a lease of shoreline property to tell the tenant about public rights to use the beach. The state's beachfront disclosure is for sales: a contract of sale or transfer of property lying wholly or partly seaward of the beachfront setback line or jurisdictional line must state that the property is or may be affected by those lines and give the local erosion rate. Whether a lease is a "transfer" isn't defined; the rule is regulatory and doesn't void a deal that leaves it out. Cautious course for a long lease of oceanfront property: include the same statement. Public beach access policy is set in the Beachfront Management Act, not in tenancy law, and local beach rules aren't covered here.

title: No Special District Disclosure in Leases
bodyText: No South Carolina statute requires a lease to disclose, or the tenant to acknowledge, that the property lies in a special purpose, improvement or assessment district. Special purpose districts (for water, sewer, fire and the like) are local governments with their own powers and reporting duties, and any charges they impose fall on the owner unless the lease passes them on. If you pass a district charge or assessment to the tenant, state it in the lease as a fee or as rent; see `edu-fees-as-rent-sc`.

title: No Steam Radiator Cover Rule
bodyText: South Carolina has no rule requiring radiator covers on request or a radiator-cover lease rider; the Code doesn't address steam radiators in rentals at all. If the unit has a steam or hot-water system you supply, you must keep it in reasonably good and safe working order and supply reasonable heat, and the common areas must be reasonably safe. Cautious course: cover exposed hot radiators in units with young children or elderly occupants if asked.

title: No Shutdown Rent Protection
bodyText: South Carolina has no rule delaying rent or eviction for government employees or contractors who aren't paid during a federal or state government shutdown. The ordinary rules apply: rent unpaid within five days of the due date, after the written notice (or the lease's bold nonpayment paragraph), lets you end the lease and file (`nonpayment-notice-sc`). Members of the armed forces and Guard on active duty have the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act protections (`edu-servicemember-rights-sc`), which don't depend on a shutdown. Cautious course: agree a written payment plan with an affected tenant.

title: Sprinkler Systems and Tenants
bodyText: South Carolina doesn't require a lease to say whether the building has a working sprinkler system, and no state law makes you retrofit sprinklers into an existing rental (any sprinkler requirement for one- and two-family homes would have to be adopted as a regulation, `edu-no-fire-sprinkler-duty-sc`). The only sprinkler notice in state law is for hotels without sprinklers, which must post one at the front desk. There is an incentive: if you install a fire sprinkler system that the law doesn't require, in a residential or commercial building, and the local taxing entity consents, you may claim a credit of 25% of the direct cost against local property taxes and an equal state income tax credit, and you may transfer an unused credit to the tenant of the site with written notice to the local taxing entity. Fire code requirements for apartment buildings come from the codes adopted locally and the State Fire Marshal (`edu-fire-code-standard-sc`).

title: Leases That Must Be in Writing
bodyText: In South Carolina a tenancy of one year or less may be created by oral agreement, and the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act treats an oral rental agreement like a written one. An agreement to occupy real estate for more than one year is void unless in writing, and an older statute gives any lease not put in writing and signed by the parties only the force of a tenancy at will, except a lease of up to one year from entry whose rent is at least two-thirds of the property's full improved value (for leases of a year or less this appears to be overtaken by the later one-year oral-tenancy rule. Assigning or surrendering a lease must be done in a writing signed by the party (or an agent authorized in writing), unless it happens by operation of law, and the general statute of frauds requires a signed writing for an agreement about an interest in land or one not to be performed within a year. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act adds a rule for a written lease only one side signed: if the other side accepts rent (or takes possession and pays) without reservation, the lease takes effect, but for no more than one year. There is no special rule for leases of five years or more. To give notice to third parties such as a later buyer or lender, a lease is recorded like a deed, and a written lease for longer than twelve months must be recorded to be valid against later buyers and creditors without notice. Cautious course: put every lease, and every lease longer than a year in particular, in writing signed by both sides.

title: Tenancies at Will
bodyText: South Carolina's older landlord-tenant chapter defines a tenant at will as anyone (other than the owner, a domestic servant or a farm laborer) occupying real estate without any agreement, oral or written, and requires a tenant at will to leave on 20 days' written notice. An oral lease longer than one year also has only the force of a tenancy at will (`edu-statute-of-frauds-lease-sc`). But most residential occupants with an agreement fall under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act instead: unless the agreement fixes a definite term, the tenancy is week to week for a roomer paying weekly rent and month to month otherwise, ended by 7 or 30 days' written notice (`edu-periodic-tenancy-notice-sc`); and a tenant who stays on with your consent after the term becomes periodic in the same way. Use the Act's notices for anyone renting a dwelling from you; use the 20-day notice only for someone occupying with no agreement at all, and for people who were never tenants consider the unlawful-occupant procedure (`edu-unauthorized-occupant-removal-sc`).

title: A Tenant's Statutory Rights to End a Lease Early
Stoves and Refrigerators
bodyText: South Carolina doesn't require you to supply a stove or refrigerator, and has no rule for a tenant who brings their own. What the Act does say: every appliance present in the unit is presumed supplied by you, so you must keep it in reasonably good and safe working order, unless the lease specifically excludes it (`appliances-excluded-sc`); and you can't exclude an appliance needed for an essential service, such as a gas range where gas is used for cooking. A unit without a landlord-provided toilet, bath or shower, refrigerator, stove and kitchen sink, where facilities are shared, makes its occupant a roomer, whose default tenancy is week to week if rent is paid weekly. If the tenant supplies their own refrigerator or stove, list it in the lease as the tenant's, with the tenant responsible for it (`appliances-included`).

title: Student Housing
bodyText: South Carolina has no student-housing statute for private landlords: no licensing, no special termination or hearing procedure, and no exemption from tenant protections for privately owned student apartments. Two rules matter: (1) residence at a public or private institution incidental to educational services (a college dormitory) is outside the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act; a private apartment rented to students is fully covered, even near campus or master-leased to students; and (2) the Fair Housing Law's sex-discrimination rule doesn't apply to renting dwellings in a single-sex dormitory property, and public colleges must give students the option to be housed only with persons of the same sex. Students under 18 can't bind themselves to a lease the way adults can (`edu-minor-tenant-filing-sc`); a parent guarantor is the usual answer. Several statutes let named public universities ground-lease land to private developers for on-campus student housing; those are university contracts, not tenancy rules.

title: Subsidy Abatement After a Failed Inspection
bodyText: No South Carolina statute or held regulation deals with abating or prorating a housing subsidy when a voucher unit fails inspection, or says whether you may charge the tenant the withheld share. For Housing Choice Voucher (Section 8) units, the federal program rules and your housing assistance payments contract with the local housing authority control: the authority can stop its payments while a Housing Quality Standards violation you are responsible for goes uncorrected, and the tenancy addendum generally bars collecting the authority's share from the tenant. Under state law the tenant still owes only the tenant's share set by the lease, and a tenant can't be evicted for the authority's failure to pay its share (`edu-no-benefit-delay-defense-sc`). Fix deficiencies within the time the authority gives.

title: Keeping Tenants' Information Confidential
bodyText: No South Carolina statute bars a landlord from disclosing information about a tenant (payment history, contact details, the fact of a tenancy) or sets a consent rule for sharing it. Two general laws apply: if you keep applicants' or tenants' personal identifying information (such as Social Security, driver's license or bank account numbers), you must notify affected South Carolina residents of a security breach without unreasonable delay; and you may not publicly post or display a Social Security number or require one to be sent over an unsecured Internet connection (`edu-tenant-records-sc`). A tenant in the state's address confidentiality program has a substitute address that public agencies must use. Cautious course: share tenant information only with the tenant's written consent, your agents and service providers, or as law or a court requires.

title: Housing for Your Employees
bodyText: The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act doesn't govern occupancy by your employee whose right to live there is conditional on employment in and about the premises (a resident manager or maintenance worker). For that arrangement no deposit, repair or notice rule of the Act applies, and no statute requires a disclosure of occupancy and vacating terms or an offer of a lease when the job ends. If the employee pays rent under an ordinary lease, or works elsewhere, the Act applies in full. When a covered employee's occupancy ends, you recover possession through the ejectment process, because the occupancy has ended; don't lock the person out. A domestic servant must vacate on 20 days' written notice. Cautious course: put the employment condition, any rent, and a vacating period in a signed writing separate from the employment terms, and return any deposit promptly.

title: Tenant Organizing
bodyText: South Carolina has no statute giving tenants a right to organize, form or join a tenants' association, or meet in common areas, and the retaliation law doesn't list organizing as protected conduct: it protects a tenant who complains to a code-enforcement agency about a health-and-safety violation, or complains to you about a violation of the Act. A rule against meetings or flyers must still meet the Act's rules test (reasonably related to tenants' convenience, safety or welfare, explicit, applied fairly), and federally assisted housing may carry federal organizing protections. Cautious course: don't take action against a tenant for joining with other tenants to raise repair complaints, since the complaints themselves are protected (`edu-retaliation-sc`).

title: Changing the Terms of a Periodic Tenancy
bodyText: South Carolina has no statute setting a notice period for changing the terms (rent or fees or anything else) of a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy, and none treating a change as needing a full termination notice. During a fixed term, terms change only as the lease allows or by written agreement. For a periodic tenancy, the cautious course is to give the change in writing at least as far ahead as the notice to end the tenancy (30 days month to month, 7 days week to week), effective at the start of a rental period, so a tenant who won't accept can leave. Rules are different: a new rule adopted mid-tenancy that substantially modifies the tenant's bargain doesn't bind a tenant who objects in writing within 30 days after notice of the right to object. The state leaves other local rules to local ordinance (`edu-local-preemption-sc`).

title: No Lease Translation Duty
bodyText: South Carolina has no rule requiring a lease to be translated into the tenant's language, even if you advertised or negotiated in another language, and prescribes no minimum type size for residential leases. The Act's only formatting rules are that the nonpayment paragraph, if used in place of a separate notice, must be in conspicuous type, and that the periodic-services entry right must be conspicuous (`edu-required-disclosures-sc`). A tenant who can't read the lease is still generally bound by it, but a court may refuse to enforce a term that was unconscionable when made (`edu-unconscionability-sc`), and national-origin discrimination is barred by the Fair Housing Law. Cautious course: if you negotiate in another language, give the tenant a courtesy translation and say in the lease which version controls.

title: No Truth-in-Renting Law
bodyText: South Carolina has no truth-in-renting act: no agency statement of rights you must give tenants, and no statute that voids a lease or awards damages because a clause misstates the law. Its rules work through the Act instead: a lease term that waives the tenant's rights, confesses judgment, or excuses or indemnifies your own liability is unenforceable, and if you deliberately use a lease with terms you know are prohibited and try to enforce them, the tenant may recover actual damages plus up to the security deposit and attorney's fees, or up to three months' rent if you act maliciously (`edu-prohibited-lease-terms-sc`). The Unfair Trade Practices Act separately bars unfair or deceptive acts in trade or commerce. Keep the lease consistent with the Act; this library's SC rows are drafted to that standard.

title: Charging Separately for Parking
bodyText: South Carolina has no rule requiring parking to be offered or priced separately from rent, and none barring it. If you charge for parking, decide in the lease whether the charge is rent or a separate fee, because the Act defines rent as consideration for use of the premises (which include grounds and facilities held out for tenants or promised to the tenant) but excludes other charges, and the five-day nonpayment route is built for rent (`edu-fees-as-rent-sc`). Cautious course: put an optional space in a separate parking agreement, say the fee isn't rent, and make loss of the space the remedy for nonpayment of the fee. The library's parking rows cover assignment and rules (`parking-ks-oh-ca`, `assigned-parking-space`, `parking-vehicle-rules`); towing is in `edu-towing-sc`.

title: Leases by a Life Tenant
bodyText: South Carolina has no civil-law usufruct, but a landlord can hold only a life estate (for example, a parent who deeded the remainder to children). A lease from a life tenant generally can't outlast the life estate unless the remainder holders join or agree, and the statutes assume the lease ends at the life tenant's death: the life tenant's executor may recover from the tenant the rent for the period up to the death (the whole installment if death falls on the due date, otherwise a proportion), and a person renting land from a life tenant who dies can't be dispossessed until that year's crop is finished, if they secure the rent. If you hold a life estate, say so in the lease and get the remainder holders' signatures if the lease should continue after your death; a tenant leasing from a life tenant should ask for that consent.

title: Discounts for Veterans and Servicemembers
bodyText: No South Carolina statute creates a rent incentive, tax credit or preference program for landlords who rent to veterans or servicemembers, and none bars you from offering one. Veteran or military status isn't a protected class under the state Fair Housing Law, so a discount offered to every qualifying veteran or servicemember is a lawful business choice; apply it by written criteria to everyone who qualifies, and record it in the lease as a rent concession (`rent-concession-wi`). Servicemembers' federal and state lease rights are in `edu-servicemember-rights-sc`.

title: Splitting Shared Utility Bills
bodyText: South Carolina has no statute or Public Service Commission rule governing how a landlord allocates a shared or master-metered utility bill among tenants (ratio billing, square-foot or occupant formulas, common-area charges), and none voids a lease term making tenants pay for service not separately metered. What applies: tenants are responsible for their own gas, electric, water, sewer and garbage service unless otherwise agreed in writing; electricity to new multi-occupancy residential buildings whose units are separately rented must be individually metered by the utility, unless the Commission approves an exception; and for buildings of four or more units on a master meter, the utility may look to you for the account. If you split a bill, put the formula in the lease, charge only the provider's actual cost, give tenants a copy of the bill, and treat the share as a charge, not rent (`edu-fees-as-rent-sc`). Whether a landlord reselling metered electricity becomes a regulated utility isn't addressed for rentals; don't mark up.

title: Utility Disclosures With the Lease
bodyText: South Carolina's one utility disclosure for a lease is the meter conservation charge: if an electricity or natural gas provider is recovering the cost of energy-efficiency improvements to the rental through a charge on the unit's account, you must give each later tenant written notice of the charge, delivered as the Act requires for notices; if you don't, the tenant may deduct from rent as the statute provides (`meter-conservation-charge-notice-sc`). No statute requires a lease attachment on utility tariffs, average bills, water or power availability, or how allocated electricity is billed. Cautious course: tell applicants which utilities they pay and roughly what they cost.

title: Interrupting Utilities You Supply or Submeter
bodyText: South Carolina has no special regime for interrupting electricity a landlord submeters or resells, but the Act covers every utility you supply. You may not wilfully interrupt essential services (electricity, running and hot water, heat, sewer, or gas used for heat, hot water or cooking) to make a tenant pay or leave; if you do, the tenant may recover possession or end the lease and recover three months' rent or twice actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees (`edu-no-rent-lockout-sc`). If you negligently or wilfully fail to provide essential services the lease or the Act requires, the tenant may, after written notice, buy reasonable service and deduct its actual cost from rent, or recover reduced-rent damages and attorney's fees. A brief planned shutoff to repair equipment isn't wilful diminution; give notice and restore service promptly. Electricity to new multi-occupancy buildings must be individually metered by the utility, so landlord-run electric submeters are rare (`edu-no-utility-apportionment-rule-sc`).

title: Utilities in the Landlord's Name
bodyText:
South Carolina has no rule requiring a utility to warn each unit before shutting off service on an account you hold, and no rule letting tenants pay your bill to keep service on or petition for a receiver.

The Act fills the gap: if the lease makes a utility yours and you negligently or wilfully fail to provide an essential service (electricity, running and hot water, heat, sewer, or gas used for heat, hot water or cooking), the tenant may, after written notice, buy reasonable service and deduct its actual cost from rent, or recover damages for the reduced rental value plus attorney's fees; a wilful shutoff is treated like a lockout.

Accounts work this way: unless otherwise agreed in writing, the tenant is responsible for their own service and you aren't liable for it, and a utility can't make you guarantee a tenant's account or refuse service because you won't, and none of these account rules applies to a building of four or more residential units served by a master meter or single connection. (One sewer regulation still allows a landlord agreement; the statute controls.)

title: When Utilities Can Cut Off Service
bodyText: For utilities the Public Service Commission regulates, South Carolina sets termination rules that protect your tenants (and you, when an account is yours). An electric or gas utility must mail a termination notice at least 10 days before cutting off service for nonpayment, try to contact the customer again shortly before, offer a deferred payment plan, and terminate only Monday to Thursday, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., unless it can take payment and reconnect. From December through March, service won't be cut off for a household member whose physician certifies a cutoff would be especially dangerous to health (renewable up to three times). Electric utilities must have written procedures for special-needs customers and for extreme heat or cold. Water utilities give 10 days' written notice and the same day-and-hour limits, and leave a door hanger after a cutoff. Utilities copy termination notices to a third party the customer names (`utility-shutoff-notice-authorization-co`). There is no general hurricane or emergency moratorium; a utility may disconnect for a public safety emergency.

title: No Submetering Disclosure Rule
bodyText: South Carolina has no statute or Public Service Commission rule requiring a lease disclosure when a landlord submeters, allocates or rebills water, sewer, gas or electricity, and no cap on such billing, billing fee or late fee for it. New multi-occupancy residential buildings get electricity through individual utility meters, so electric submetering is mostly limited to older buildings and Commission-approved exceptions. If you bill tenants for any utility, the lease is your only tool: name each utility you bill, the method (submeter reading or formula), the billing schedule, and that you'll pass through only the provider's actual charge with a copy of the bill. Tenants are otherwise responsible for their own accounts unless agreed in writing (`edu-utilities-sc`). See `edu-no-utility-apportionment-rule-sc` for shared bills.

title: Water Heater Temperature Settings
bodyText: No South Carolina statute or held regulation requires you to set a rental unit's water heater to a maximum temperature before a new tenant moves in. The temperature limits in state rules (hot water at fixtures between 100 and 120 degrees Fahrenheit) apply to licensed care facilities such as residential care and nursing homes, not apartments. Your duty under the Act is to make reasonable amounts of hot water available at all times (unless the unit's own heater is under the tenant's exclusive control on a direct utility connection) and to keep the water heater in reasonably good and safe working order. Cautious course: set tank thermostats to about 120 degrees at each turnover to reduce scald risk, and tell the tenant how to adjust it.

title: Window Guards and Security Bars
bodyText: South Carolina has no statute or held regulation requiring window guards where young children live, a window-guard lease notice, or rules for burglar or security bars (such as a quick-release requirement or a disclosure of how the bars open). Building and fire codes adopted locally govern emergency escape openings, so bars that can't be opened from inside on a sleeping-room window may violate the code (local matters aren't covered here). Under the Act you must comply with codes materially affecting health and safety and keep the unit fit and safe. Cautious course: use only bars with an inside quick-release on bedroom windows, show tenants how they open, and consider window stops in upper-floor units with children.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: South Carolina follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (S.C. Code Ann. § 36-3-311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (S.C. Code Ann. § 36-1-308(b)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. South Carolina adopted this rule in 2008 (2008 Act No. 204), so it governs checks offered from July 1, 2008. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: South Carolina's landlord-tenant act imposes a duty of good faith: every duty under the chapter, and every act that must be done before using a right or remedy under it, carries an obligation of good faith in its performance or enforcement (S.C. Code Ann. § 27-40-220). That binds you and the tenant alike. 'Good faith' means honesty in fact in the conduct of the transaction concerned (S.C. Code Ann. § 27-40-210(5)). In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.
